core.h: Cross: group AB x group O
core.p: This cross is a favourite because the children can be neither of the parents' blood groups. The AB parent (IAIB) produces gametes IA and IB; the O parent (IOIO) produces only IO gametes.
bullets: Gametes: IA, IB (from AB parent) and IO, IO (from O parent)
Offspring genotypes: IAIO, IAIO, IBIO, IBIO
Offspring phenotypes: 2 group A : 2 group B, so a ratio of **1 A : 1 B**
Probability of a group A child = **1/2 (50%)**; group B = **1/2**
Probability of a group AB or group O child = **0**
The children are all **heterozygous**, so they all carry IO

callouts.p: An AB parent and an O parent can never have an AB or an O child.

core.h: Other crosses you should be able to do
core.p: Practise the common combinations until you can predict results quickly. The table shows the outcomes, each worked out with a Punnett square.
bullets: Two group O parents (IOIO x IOIO) can only have **group O** children
Two group AB parents (IAIB x IAIB) give **1 A : 2 AB : 1 B**
IAIA x IBIB gives **all group AB** children
IAIO x IAIO gives **3 group A : 1 group O** (just like a normal dominant/recessive cross)
IAIB x IAIO gives IAIA, IAIO, IAIB, IBIO: **2 A : 1 AB : 1 B**

core.p: Many 4 and 6 mark questions give you the blood groups of a family and ask you to deduce the genotypes. Use the children to work out hidden IO alleles in the parents.
bullets: A **group O child** (IOIO) must have received IO from **each** parent, so both parents must carry IO
So if a group A parent has a group O child, that parent must be **IAIO**, not IAIA
A **group AB child** must have received IA from one parent and IB from the other
A group AB parent cannot have a group O child, because the AB parent has no IO to pass on
Use the phrase 'must have inherited one allele from each parent' in your explanation

callouts.p: For a 'deduce' question, state the clue (for example, the child is group O), what it means (child is IOIO), and the conclusion (so each parent passed on IO).

core.p: A Punnett square shows the **probability** of each genotype in **each** pregnancy. Fertilisation is random, so the actual numbers in a real family may not match the predicted ratio, especially in small families.
bullets: Each child is an **independent event**: the chance does not change with earlier children
If parents IAIO x IBIO already have a group O child, the next child still has a **1/4** chance of being group O
Express probability as a fraction (1/4), decimal (0.25) or percentage (25%), not as '1 in 4 chance' and '25%' combined in a muddle
A ratio (such as 1 : 1 : 1 : 1) is not the same as a probability

callouts.p: Students often say that after three group A children the fourth must be group O. This is wrong: each fertilisation is random and independent.

core.p: Knowing ABO blood groups matters in medicine. People make **antibodies** in their plasma against the antigens they do **not** have. If blood with the wrong antigens is transfused, the antibodies bind to the antigens and make the donated red blood cells **clump together (agglutinate)**, which can be fatal.
bullets: Group A people have **anti-B** antibodies; group B people have **anti-A** antibodies
Group AB people have **neither** antibody, so they can receive A, B, AB or O red cells
Group O people have **both anti-A and anti-B** antibodies, so they can only receive group O blood
Group O red cells have **no A or B antigens**, so they can be given to people of any ABO group in an emergency
This explains why hospitals test and match blood before a transfusion

callouts.t: Antigens on cells, antibodies in plasma
callouts.p: Antigens are on the red blood cell membrane; antibodies are dissolved in the plasma. Do not mix them up.

core.h: Linking ABO to the rest of genetics
core.p: ABO inheritance follows the same rules as every monohybrid cross, which is why it is a good test of your understanding of key genetic terms.
bullets: The ABO gene is found at the same position on a **pair of homologous chromosomes**
During **meiosis**, the two alleles separate so each gamete gets **one** allele
**Random fertilisation** decides which allele from each parent the child receives
Different **alleles** are different versions of the same gene, caused originally by **mutations** in the DNA base sequence
Codominance and multiple alleles are exceptions to Mendel's simple 'one dominant, one recessive' pattern, but the alleles are still inherited in exactly the way Mendel described

analogy.p: Think of each red blood cell as a jacket and each allele as an instruction to sew on a badge. IA says 'sew on a triangle badge', IB says 'sew on a square badge' and IO is a blank instruction card that says nothing. You get two instruction cards, one from each parent. With IA and IB you sew on both badges (codominance: both instructions are followed). With IA and IO you only sew on a triangle, because the blank card adds nothing (IO is recessive). With two blank cards the jacket has no badges at all (group O). There are three kinds of card in the population (multiple alleles) but you only ever hold two. Where it breaks down: real alleles do not 'decide' anything; they are DNA sequences coding for enzymes that attach antigen molecules, and a recessive allele is not always a 'blank': it may code for a protein that does not work.

terms.d: A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein.
A different form (version) of the same gene.
When a gene has more than two alleles in a population; each individual carries only two of them.
When both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype.
An allele that is expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed in the phenotype when two copies are present (no dominant allele).
The combination of alleles an organism has for a gene, for example IAIO.
The observable characteristic produced by the genotype (and environment), for example blood group A.
Having two identical alleles of a gene, for example IBIB or IOIO.
Having two different alleles of a gene, for example IAIO or IAIB.
A molecule (protein or glycoprotein) on the surface of a cell; in ABO it is antigen A or B on red blood cells.
A protein in the plasma that binds to a specific antigen.
A haploid sex cell (sperm or egg) containing one allele of each gene.
A grid used to show all possible combinations of gametes from two parents and the probability of each offspring genotype.
Variation where individuals fall into distinct categories with no intermediates, such as ABO blood group.
Clumping together of red blood cells when antibodies bind to the antigens on them.

mistakes.w: A person has three alleles for blood group.
mistakes.r: There are three alleles in the population (multiple alleles), but each person has only two.

mistakes.w: Blood group AB is a blend of A and B.
mistakes.r: IA and IB are codominant: both alleles are expressed, so both antigen A and antigen B are produced.

mistakes.w: IO is dominant because group O is the most common blood group.
mistakes.r: IO is recessive to both IA and IB; how common an allele is does not tell you whether it is dominant.

mistakes.w: A group A person must be IAIA.
mistakes.r: Group A can be IAIA or IAIO; you need family information to decide.

mistakes.w: Using A and a, or A, B and O as allele symbols.
mistakes.r: Use IA, IB and IO (or the symbols given), with a key.

mistakes.w: Writing gametes as IAIO.
mistakes.r: Gametes are haploid and carry one allele: IA or IO.

mistakes.w: Two group A parents cannot have a group O child.
mistakes.r: If both parents are IAIO there is a 1/4 chance of an IOIO (group O) child.

mistakes.w: After three group A children the next one must be group O.
mistakes.r: Each fertilisation is random and independent, so the probability is the same for every child.

mistakes.w: Group AB people have antibodies against A and B.
mistakes.r: AB people have neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies; group O people have both.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term multiple alleles.
model: A gene that has more than two alleles (in the population)
exam.tip: You can add 'each person has only two' but the key idea is more than two alleles.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by codominance, using blood group AB as an example.
model: Both alleles in the heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype
Genotype IAIB produces both antigen A and antigen B (so the person is group AB)
exam.tip: Link the definition to the example to get both marks.

exam.q: Give all the possible genotypes of a person with blood group B.
model: IBIB and IBIO (both needed)
exam.tip: Two genotypes for one mark: missing one loses the mark.

exam.q: How many different genotypes and phenotypes are possible for the ABO blood group gene?
model: Six genotypes
Four phenotypes
exam.tip: Remember the IO allele is hidden in IAIO and IBIO.

exam.q: A man is blood group AB and a woman is blood group O. Use a genetic diagram to determine the possible blood groups of their children and the probability of each.
model: Parents' genotypes IAIB and IOIO
Gametes IA, IB and IO
Offspring genotypes IAIO and IBIO
Group A probability 0.5 and group B probability 0.5 (no AB or O)
exam.tip: Show gametes separately; examiners give a mark for correct gametes even if the final answer is wrong.

exam.q: Two parents have blood groups A and B. Their first child is blood group O. Explain the genotypes of both parents.
model: Child must be IOIO
Child inherits one allele from each parent, so each parent must carry IO
Mother/father group A is IAIO and the other parent group B is IBIO
exam.tip: Start from the child: group O can only be IOIO.

exam.q: The parents in the question above have a second child. Calculate the probability that this child will have blood group AB.
model: Cross IAIO x IBIO gives IAIB, IAIO, IBIO, IOIO
Probability of IAIB = 1/4 (0.25 or 25%)
exam.tip: The first child's blood group does not change the probability for the second.

exam.q: A woman says her group AB son could not be the child of a group O man. Evaluate this claim.
model: The group O man is IOIO so can only pass on IO
A group AB son must be IAIB, needing IA from one parent and IB from the other
So the man cannot be the biological father; the claim is correct
exam.tip: Evaluate means reach a judgement, so finish with a conclusion.

exam.q: Explain why a person with blood group O can donate red blood cells to a person with any ABO blood group, but can only receive group O blood.
model: Group O red blood cells have no A or B antigens
So the recipient's antibodies have nothing to bind to and the cells do not clump/agglutinate
Group O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies
These would bind to A or B antigens on donated A, B or AB cells, causing agglutination
exam.tip: Keep antigens on cells and antibodies in plasma clearly separate.

exam.q: Two parents are both blood group AB. Determine the ratio of blood groups expected in their children.
model: Gametes IA and IB from each parent
Offspring IAIA, IAIB, IAIB, IBIB
Ratio 1 A : 2 AB : 1 B
exam.tip: Group O is impossible because neither parent has IO.

exam.q: Explain how the inheritance of ABO blood groups differs from the inheritance of a characteristic controlled by one dominant and one recessive allele, and how it is similar. Use genetic diagrams in your answer.
model: ABO has three alleles in the population (multiple alleles) instead of two
IA and IB are codominant so the heterozygote IAIB expresses both (group AB), unlike a heterozygote with a dominant allele where only the dominant is seen
IO is recessive to IA and IB, just as a recessive allele is in simple dominance
Similar: each person has two alleles and gametes carry one, separated in meiosis
Similar: alleles combine at random fertilisation and Punnett squares predict probabilities
Correct diagram, e.g. IAIO x IBIO giving 1 AB : 1 A : 1 B : 1 O compared with Aa x Aa giving 3 dominant : 1 recessive
exam.tip: A 6 mark answer must cover both differences and similarities, with at least one correct diagram.

worked.q: A group A father (IAIO) and a group AB mother have a child. What is the probability that the child is group B?
steps: Father's gametes: IA or IO
Mother is IAIB, so her gametes are IA or IB
Punnett square: IAIA, IAIB, IAIO, IBIO
Phenotypes: A, AB, A, B
Only IBIO is group B: 1 out of 4

worked.q: In a family, grandfather is group O and grandmother is group A. Their daughter is group A and she has a child with a group B man; the child is group O. Deduce the genotypes of the daughter and the group B man.
steps: The child is group O, so must be IOIO
The child received IO from each parent
So the daughter (group A) is IAIO and the man (group B) is IBIO
Check: the daughter's IO could have come from her group O father (IOIO), who can only give IO, so this is consistent
In fact any child of the grandfather must receive IO from him, so the daughter has to be IAIO anyway
worked.ans: Daughter IAIO; group B man IBIO

worked.q: A couple with genotypes IAIA and IBIO want to know the chance of having two children who are both group AB.
steps: Gametes: IA only from the first parent; IB or IO from the second
Offspring: IAIB (AB) or IAIO (A), each with probability 1/2
Each child is an independent event
Probability both are AB = 1/2 x 1/2

bio_edx.2.12.summary: A **sex-linked** characteristic is controlled by a gene carried on a sex chromosome, usually the **X chromosome**. The Y chromosome is much smaller and lacks most of the genes found on the X, so a male (XY) has only **one** allele for an X-linked gene. This means a single **recessive** allele, such as the one causing **haemophilia** or **red-green colour blindness**, is always expressed in males, while females (XX) need two copies and are usually **carriers**. You must be able to explain this pattern and use genetic diagrams and pedigrees to predict probabilities.

core.p: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; one pair, the **sex chromosomes**, decides sex. Females are **XX** and males are **XY**. The X chromosome is large and carries many genes not linked to sex at all, such as genes for blood clotting proteins and colour vision. The Y chromosome is small and carries few genes, including the gene that triggers male development.
bullets: Female = **XX**; male = **XY**
Eggs always carry an **X**; sperm carry **either X or Y** (50 : 50)
The **father decides the sex** of the child by passing on X (girl) or Y (boy)
The Y chromosome has **no matching allele** for most genes on the X
So males have only **one copy** of most X-linked genes, while females have **two**

callouts.p: A characteristic controlled by a gene (allele) located on a sex chromosome, usually the X chromosome.

fig.cap: The X chromosome is much larger than the Y. A sex-linked gene such as the one for a blood clotting factor sits on the X; the Y has no matching allele, so a male has only one allele for the gene.

core.h: Why recessive X-linked disorders affect more males
core.p: This is the central idea of the spec point. Most sex-linked disorders are caused by a **recessive allele on the X chromosome**. A female has two X chromosomes, so a dominant normal allele on her other X can mask the faulty one. A male has only one X and the Y carries no allele to mask it, so **one recessive allele is enough** for him to have the disorder.
bullets: Male with **XhY** has the disorder: there is **no second allele** on the Y to mask h
Female with **XHXh** does **not** have the disorder but is a **carrier**
A female is only affected if she is **XhXh**, which needs an affected (or carrier-allele) father **and** a carrier (or affected) mother
The chance of a female being homozygous recessive is much lower, so the disorders are **far more common in males**
Males cannot be carriers: they either have the disorder or they do not

callouts.p: The phrase the mark scheme wants: 'males have only one X chromosome / the Y chromosome does not carry the gene, so a single recessive allele is expressed'.

core.p: Because the gene is on the X chromosome, the allele is written as a **superscript on the X**. The Y is written with no allele, because it does not carry the gene. This makes it obvious which chromosome carries the allele and stops you giving males two alleles.
bullets: **XH** = X chromosome with the dominant, normal allele
**Xh** = X chromosome with the recessive, disorder allele
**Y** = Y chromosome, written with **no** allele
Female genotypes: XHXH (normal), XHXh (carrier), XhXh (affected)
Male genotypes: XHY (normal), XhY (affected)
Always write a key, for example H = normal clotting, h = haemophilia

callouts.p: Writing an allele on the Y (such as XHYh) is wrong for X-linked genes and loses marks.

core.p: **Haemophilia** is a sex-linked recessive disorder in which the **blood does not clot properly**, because the person cannot make enough of a protein (a **clotting factor**) needed for clotting. Even small cuts or internal bruises can bleed for a long time.
bullets: Caused by a **recessive allele on the X chromosome**
Symptoms: **prolonged bleeding** after injury, bleeding into joints and muscles
Treated by **injections of the missing clotting factor**
Much more common in **males** than in females
Famous example: it was passed through Queen Victoria's descendants into several European royal families, appearing mostly in sons

callouts.p: A sex-linked (X-linked) recessive disorder in which the blood fails to clot normally because a clotting factor is missing.

core.p: **Red-green colour blindness** is another sex-linked recessive condition. The allele affects a pigment protein in cone cells of the retina, so the person finds it hard to tell red and green apart.
bullets: Caused by a **recessive allele on the X chromosome**
Affected person has difficulty **distinguishing red from green**
Roughly **1 in 12 men** but only about **1 in 200 women** are affected, which shows the male bias clearly
Like haemophilia, it is inherited using exactly the same X-linked genetic diagrams

callouts.p: Exams may use an unfamiliar sex-linked disorder (for example Duchenne muscular dystrophy). Apply the same rules: recessive allele on the X, males need one copy, females need two.

core.p: A **carrier** is a person who has **one copy of a recessive allele** but does **not** show the disorder because a dominant allele masks it. For X-linked disorders only **females** can be carriers, because only they have two X chromosomes.
bullets: Carrier genotype: **XHXh**
A carrier mother passes Xh in **half** her eggs
So each son of a carrier mother has a **1/2** chance of being affected
Each daughter of a carrier mother (with a normal father) has a **1/2** chance of being a carrier
Carrier females can be identified only from family history or a genetic test, because they look unaffected

callouts.p: An individual who has one recessive allele for a disorder but does not have the disorder, because a dominant allele is also present.

core.h: Cross 1: carrier mother x unaffected father
core.p: This is the most frequently examined cross. The mother is XHXh and the father is XHY. Draw the gametes first: the mother can give XH or Xh; the father can give XH or Y.
bullets: Offspring: XHXH, XHXh, XHY, XhY
**1 in 4 (25%)** of all children is an **affected son**
**1 in 2 (50%)** of sons are affected
**No daughters** are affected; **1 in 2 (50%)** of daughters are carriers
Ratio: 1 unaffected girl : 1 carrier girl : 1 unaffected boy : 1 affected boy

callouts.p: 'Probability that a child is an affected boy' = 1/4. 'Probability that a son is affected' (we already know it is a boy) = 1/2. These are different questions.

fig.cap: Carrier mother (XHXh) and unaffected father (XHY). The only affected child is a son (XhY), with a probability of 1/4 for any child, or 1/2 for a son. Half the daughters are carriers.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='200' y='18' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Parents: XHXh x XHY</text><text x='220' y='38' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>Father's gametes</text><text x='175' y='54' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>XH</text><text x='265' y='54' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>Y</text><text x='52' y='128' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>Mother's eggs</text><text x='114' y='96' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>XH</text><text x='114' y='156' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>Xh</text><rect x='130' y='60' width='90' height='60' fill='#bbf7d0' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='220' y='60' width='90' height='60' fill='#bbf7d0' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='130' y='120' width='90' height='60' fill='#fde68a' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='220' y='120' width='90' height='60' fill='#fecaca' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='175' y='88' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>XHXH</text><text x='175' y='105' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#15803d'>normal girl</text><text x='265' y='88' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>XHY</text><text x='265' y='105' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#15803d'>normal boy</text><text x='175' y='148' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>XHXh</text><text x='175' y='165' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b45309'>carrier girl</text><text x='265' y='148' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>XhY</text><text x='265' y='165' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>affected boy</text><text x='200' y='204' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Affected child: 1/4</text><text x='200' y='224' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Sons affected: 1/2</text></svg>

core.h: Cross 2: affected father x unaffected (non-carrier) mother
core.p: The father is XhY and the mother is XHXH. A father passes his **X to every daughter** and his **Y to every son**, so this cross gives a very distinctive result.
bullets: Offspring: XHXh, XHXh, XHY, XHY
**All daughters are carriers** (they all receive the father's Xh)
**All sons are unaffected** (they receive the father's Y, not his X)
An affected father **can never pass the disorder to his son**: there is no father-to-son transmission of X-linked disorders
The disorder can then reappear in the next generation in the daughters' sons, so it seems to 'skip a generation'

callouts.t: Sons get their X from mum
callouts.p: A boy always inherits his X chromosome from his mother and his Y from his father, so an X-linked disorder in a son always comes from the mother.

fig.cap: Affected father (XhY) and non-carrier mother (XHXH). Every daughter receives the father's Xh and is a carrier; every son receives his Y and is unaffected.

core.h: Cross 3: how an affected female arises
core.p: A female can only be affected (XhXh) if she inherits Xh from **both** parents. Her father must therefore be **affected** (XhY), because a male's only X carries his phenotype, and her mother must be a **carrier** or affected.
bullets: Carrier mother XHXh x affected father XhY
Offspring: XHXh (carrier girl), XhXh (affected girl), XHY (normal boy), XhY (affected boy)
Probability of an affected child = **1/2**
Probability that a daughter is affected = **1/2**
If a female is affected, **all her sons** will be affected, because every son gets one of her X chromosomes and both carry h

callouts.p: Clues in a pedigree: mostly males affected, no father-to-son passing, affected males often have unaffected parents (carrier mothers), and affected females always have an affected father.

core.p: A **family pedigree** shows how a characteristic passes through generations. Squares are males, circles are females, shaded shapes are affected individuals, and a horizontal line joining a male and female shows parents. Carriers are sometimes shown with a dot or half shading.
bullets: Generations are labelled with Roman numerals (I, II, III)
A vertical line from the parents leads to a horizontal line linking their children
To find genotypes: start with **affected males (XhY)** because their genotype is certain
An unaffected male must be **XHY**
The mother of an affected son must have at least one Xh, so if she is unaffected she is a **carrier (XHXh)**
The daughter of an affected father must have received Xh, so she is at least a carrier

callouts.p: In 'explain' questions quote the individuals by number, for example 'individual 5 is affected but her parents 1 and 2 are not, so...'.

core.p: Grade 9 answers often compare X-linked inheritance with a normal (autosomal) recessive disorder such as cystic fibrosis. The key difference is that for autosomal genes males and females both have two alleles.
bullets: Autosomal recessive: affects males and females **equally**
X-linked recessive: affects **males far more often**
Autosomal: both sexes can be carriers; X-linked: **only females** can be carriers
Autosomal: father can pass the allele to sons; X-linked: **never father to son**
Both: an affected child can have two unaffected parents

core.p: Families with a history of a sex-linked disorder may be offered **genetic counselling**, where Punnett squares and pedigrees are used to estimate the risk for future children. Each pregnancy is an **independent** event, so the probability is the same every time.
bullets: A known carrier woman has a **1/4** chance of an affected child with an unaffected partner
Her risk for each **son** is **1/2**
Testing can show whether a woman is a carrier
Probabilities can be given as fractions, decimals or percentages, or ratios when asked
Real families may not match predicted ratios because fertilisation is random and families are small

callouts.p: A 1 in 4 chance does not mean one child in every four will be affected; each child has the same 1/4 chance.

analogy.p: Think of the X chromosome as a car tyre that might have a puncture (the recessive allele). Females have two X chromosomes, like a car with a spare tyre: if one tyre is punctured, the spare (the dominant allele) keeps the car running, so she is a carrier but not affected. Males have one X and a Y; the Y is like a tiny toolkit that has no spare tyre in it at all. If his one tyre is punctured, the car cannot run properly, so he is affected. Where it breaks down: in a real female both X chromosomes are present in her cells at the same time (one is not kept in reserve), and the 'puncture' is a DNA sequence change that stops a protein such as a clotting factor working, not damage that can be repaired.

terms.d: The pair of chromosomes that determine sex: XX in females and XY in males.
Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome (pairs 1 to 22 in humans).
A gene located on a sex chromosome, usually the X chromosome.
An inherited disorder caused by a faulty allele on a sex chromosome, such as haemophilia or red-green colour blindness.
Inherited through a recessive allele on the X chromosome; expressed in males with one copy and in females only with two copies.
An individual with one recessive allele who does not show the disorder because a dominant allele is present.
A sex-linked recessive disorder in which the blood does not clot properly because a clotting factor is missing.
A sex-linked recessive condition in which a person cannot easily distinguish red from green.
A different form of the same gene.
An allele that is expressed even when only one copy is present.
An allele that is expressed only when no dominant allele is present.
Having two identical alleles of a gene, for example XHXH or XhXh.
Having two different alleles of a gene, for example XHXh.
The alleles an individual has, for example XhY.
The characteristic shown by an individual, for example having haemophilia.
A diagram showing the inheritance of a characteristic through generations of a family.

mistakes.w: Males are more likely to have haemophilia because the allele is on the Y chromosome.
mistakes.r: The allele is on the X chromosome; males have only one X and the Y has no allele to mask it.

mistakes.w: Males can be carriers of haemophilia.
mistakes.r: Males have only one allele, so they are either affected (XhY) or unaffected (XHY); only females can be carriers.

mistakes.w: Writing male genotypes as XHYh or Hh.
mistakes.r: Write XHY or XhY; the Y chromosome carries no allele for the gene.

mistakes.w: An affected father passes haemophilia to his son.
mistakes.r: A father passes his Y, not his X, to a son, so an X-linked allele in a son always comes from the mother.

mistakes.w: Probability that a son is affected is 1/4 (carrier mother x normal father).
mistakes.r: 1/4 of all children are affected sons; of the sons alone, 1/2 are affected.

mistakes.w: Females can never have haemophilia.
mistakes.r: Females can be affected (XhXh) if they inherit Xh from an affected father and a carrier or affected mother; it is just rare.

mistakes.w: Sex-linked means a disorder only found in one sex.
mistakes.r: Sex-linked means the gene is on a sex chromosome; both sexes can inherit it, though one is affected more often.

mistakes.w: Haemophilia means you have no blood platelets.
mistakes.r: Haemophilia is caused by a missing clotting factor protein, so blood does not clot properly.

exam.q: State what is meant by a sex-linked disorder.
model: A disorder caused by an allele on a sex chromosome (usually the X chromosome)
exam.tip: 'On the X chromosome' is enough for the mark.

exam.q: Give one example of a sex-linked genetic disorder in humans.
model: Haemophilia / red-green colour blindness (accept Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
exam.tip: Do not give cystic fibrosis: that gene is on an autosome.

exam.q: Explain why haemophilia is more common in males than in females.
model: The allele is recessive and found on the X chromosome
Males have only one X chromosome / the Y chromosome does not carry the gene
So one recessive allele is expressed in males, whereas females need two recessive alleles (so heterozygous females are carriers)
exam.tip: Three ideas: recessive, on the X, no matching allele on the Y.

exam.q: Explain why a man with haemophilia cannot pass the disorder to his son.
model: A son inherits the Y chromosome from his father
The haemophilia allele is on the X chromosome, which the son inherits from his mother
exam.tip: Mention both chromosomes: Y from father, X from mother.

exam.q: A woman who is a carrier of red-green colour blindness has children with a man with normal colour vision. Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that a child will be a colour-blind boy.
model: Parents XBXb and XBY (with key)
Gametes XB, Xb and XB, Y
Offspring XBXB, XBY, XBXb, XbY
Probability of a colour-blind boy = 1/4 (0.25 or 25%)
exam.tip: Define your symbols and show the gametes for full marks.

exam.q: The couple above have a son. What is the probability that he is colour-blind?
exam.tip: We already know the child is a boy, so only the two male boxes count.

exam.q: A man with haemophilia has children with a woman who is not a carrier. Describe the expected phenotypes of their sons and daughters.
model: All sons are unaffected (XHY)
All daughters are carriers (XHXh)
Daughters are unaffected because they also inherit XH from the mother
exam.tip: Carriers are unaffected: say both their genotype and phenotype.

exam.q: Explain how a girl could be born with haemophilia.
model: She must be homozygous recessive (XhXh)
She must inherit Xh from her father, so he must have haemophilia
And Xh from her mother, so her mother must be a carrier or affected
exam.tip: Link each Xh to the parent it came from.

exam.q: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected son. Deduce the genotypes of the parents and explain your reasoning.
model: The son is XhY and received his X from his mother
So the unaffected mother must be a carrier XHXh
The unaffected father must be XHY (males show their single allele)
exam.tip: Start from the individual whose genotype is certain.

exam.q: Compare the inheritance of haemophilia with the inheritance of cystic fibrosis, a recessive disorder caused by an allele on chromosome 7.
model: Both are caused by recessive alleles, so heterozygotes are unaffected carriers
Both can appear in a child of two unaffected parents
Cystic fibrosis allele is on an autosome, so males and females have two alleles and are affected about equally
Haemophilia allele is on the X chromosome; males have only one allele, so are affected much more often
For cystic fibrosis both sexes can be carriers; for haemophilia only females can be carriers
Cystic fibrosis can pass from father to son, haemophilia cannot; genetic diagrams use Ff notation for CF but XHXh / XhY for haemophilia
exam.tip: A compare question needs similarities and differences linked with 'whereas'.

worked.q: A woman whose father had haemophilia marries an unaffected man. Her own phenotype is normal. Calculate the probability that their first child is an affected boy, and the probability that their first son is affected.
steps: Her father was XhY, and every daughter receives her father's X, so she must have received Xh
She is unaffected, so she is a carrier: XHXh
The man is unaffected, so XHY
Gametes: XH or Xh (mother); XH or Y (father)
Offspring: XHXH, XHY, XHXh, XhY
Affected boy = 1 of 4 boxes = 1/4
Of the 2 boys, 1 is affected = 1/2
worked.ans: Affected boy: 1/4 (25%); a son being affected: 1/2 (50%)

worked.q: A colour-blind woman has children with a man with normal colour vision. Predict the phenotypes of their children.
steps: Key: B = normal colour vision, b = colour blindness
Woman is colour-blind so XbXb; man is XBY
Gametes: Xb only (mother); XB or Y (father)
Offspring: XBXb and XbY
Every daughter receives XB from her father, so is a carrier with normal vision
Every son receives Xb from his mother and Y from his father, so is colour-blind
worked.ans: All sons colour-blind; all daughters have normal vision but are carriers

bio_edx.2.13.summary: Simple genetic diagrams follow one gene with two alleles, but **most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance**, which is why characteristics such as height and skin colour show **continuous variation**. Differences between individuals come from two sources: **genetic variation** (different alleles, produced by **mutation** and shuffled by **sexual reproduction**) and **environmental variation** (differences caused by an organism's **interaction with its environment**, such as diet, climate or light). Most features are caused by **both** acting together.

core.p: **Variation** is the differences in characteristics between individuals. Variation **within a species** (for example between people) is caused by differences in their genes, their environment, or both. At GCSE you need to explain where these differences come from and why most characteristics are not as simple as a Punnett square suggests.
bullets: **Phenotype** = the characteristics an organism shows
**Genotype** = the alleles it has
Phenotype is the result of **genotype interacting with the environment**
Variation between members of the same species is the raw material for **natural selection** and **evolution**
There is usually **extensive genetic variation** within a population of a species

callouts.p: Phenotype = genotype + environment (both usually contribute).

core.h: Most features are controlled by multiple genes
core.p: Mendel's pea crosses and simple Punnett squares study characteristics controlled by **a single gene**. In reality, **most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes** rather than single gene inheritance. Characteristics controlled by many genes are described as **polygenic**. Each gene adds a small effect, and the effects add together.
bullets: Examples of features controlled by many genes: **height**, **body mass**, **skin colour**, **eye colour**, **intelligence**, susceptibility to heart disease
Very few human characteristics are controlled by one gene, for example **ABO blood group** and some inherited disorders such as **cystic fibrosis**
Each of the genes involved may have several alleles, so huge numbers of genotype combinations are possible
That is why children of the same parents can look very different from each other
Eye colour is often used as a simple single-gene example, but it is actually controlled by several genes, which is why there are many shades

callouts.p: Most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance.

callouts.t: Single gene examples are the exception
callouts.p: Do not say most characteristics are controlled by one dominant and one recessive allele; that is only true for a few.

core.h: Why multiple genes give continuous variation
core.p: If a feature is controlled by one gene with two alleles, there are only a few possible phenotypes (for example tall or short). If it is controlled by **many genes**, each adding a little, the number of possible combinations grows rapidly. Most people get a mixture of 'more' and 'less' alleles, so most end up in the middle and a few at the extremes. This produces a **bell-shaped (normal) distribution** and **continuous variation**.
bullets: One gene: few distinct categories, **discontinuous** variation
Two genes: already 5 categories in a ratio of 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1
Many genes: so many categories that they merge into a **smooth range**
The environment then blurs the categories even more (for example diet affecting height)
Result: characteristics like height can take **any value within a range**

callouts.p: Explain the shape of the graph: more genes means more combinations, and most combinations are intermediate, so most individuals are near the mean.

core.p: The type of variation shows up in how data is collected and plotted. **Discontinuous** data falls into distinct groups and is shown on a **bar chart**. **Continuous** data can take any value in a range and is shown on a **histogram** (or line graph), often forming a normal distribution.
bullets: Discontinuous: **distinct categories**, no in-betweens, usually **one or a few genes**, little or no environmental effect (e.g. blood group, tongue rolling as a classroom example)
Continuous: **range of values**, usually **many genes plus the environment** (e.g. height, mass, hand span, leaf length)
Discontinuous data: bar chart with gaps between bars
Continuous data: histogram with no gaps, grouped into class intervals

core.h: Genetic variation: where new alleles come from (mutation)
core.p: **Genetic variation** means different characteristics as a result of having **different alleles**. The original source of all new alleles is **mutation**: a rare, random change in the **base sequence of DNA**. A mutation in a gene creates a new allele, which may be passed on if it happens in cells that make gametes.
bullets: Mutation = a **random change in the DNA base sequence**
Mutations create **new alleles** and are the **only source of new genetic variation**
Most mutations have **no effect** on the phenotype; some are harmful; a few are **beneficial**
Only mutations in **gametes** (or cells that make them) are **inherited** by offspring
Mutation rate can be increased by **ionising radiation** and some **chemicals**

callouts.p: Different characteristics as a result of mutation or sexual reproduction.

core.p: **Sexual reproduction** does not make new alleles, but it produces **new combinations** of existing alleles, so every offspring (except identical twins) has a unique genotype. This happens in two ways.
bullets: **Meiosis** produces genetically different gametes: chromosome pairs are separated **randomly**, so each gamete gets a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes
**Random fertilisation**: any one of millions of sperm can fuse with an egg, combining two sets of chromosomes from **two different parents**
Together these produce **enormous variety** among offspring of the same parents
Asexual reproduction produces **clones** with no genetic variation (apart from mutations)
Genetic variation within a species allows some individuals to survive changes in the environment

callouts.p: Mutation makes new alleles; sexual reproduction makes new combinations of alleles. Exam answers that say sexual reproduction 'creates new genes' lose the mark.

core.p: **Environmental variation** means different characteristics caused by an organism's **interaction with its environment**. The environment includes everything around the organism: food, climate, light, soil, disease, and for humans, lifestyle and culture. Environmental changes to the phenotype are **not inherited**, because they do not change the DNA in gametes.
bullets: Humans: **diet** (affects body mass and height), **exercise** (muscle size), **sunlight** (sun tan), **accidents** (scars), **language** and **accent**, hair styles, tattoos
Plants: **light intensity** (height, leaf size, colour), **soil minerals** and **water** (growth), **temperature**
Leaves on the shaded side of a tree are often larger than leaves in full sun
Plants grown in the dark are tall, thin and yellow; plants lacking magnesium have yellow leaves
Some characteristics are caused only by the environment, for example **scars** or the **language** you speak

callouts.p: Different characteristics caused by an organism's interaction with the environment.
A body builder's large muscles or a scar are not passed to children, because the alleles in the gametes have not changed.

core.p: Most characteristics are affected by **both** genes and the environment. Your genes set a **potential** (a possible range); the environment decides where within that range you end up. For example, you may inherit alleles for being tall, but if you are badly undernourished as a child you will not reach that height.
bullets: **Height**: many genes set the potential; diet and health in childhood affect the actual height
**Body mass**: genes affect metabolism; diet and exercise change mass
**Skin colour**: many genes set the base colour; sunlight causes tanning
**Risk of diseases** such as heart disease and some cancers: genes increase risk; smoking, diet and exercise also matter
**Plant height**: genes plus light, water, minerals and temperature

callouts.p: The environment cannot make you grow beyond your genetic potential, but it can stop you reaching it.

fig.cap: The causes of variation. Genetic variation comes from mutation, which makes new alleles, and sexual reproduction (meiosis and random fertilisation), which makes new combinations. Environmental variation comes from an organism's interaction with its surroundings. Most features result from both.

core.p: **Identical twins** form when one fertilised egg splits into two embryos, so they have **identical genotypes**. Any difference between them must be caused by the **environment**. Scientists compare identical twins brought up apart with those brought up together to estimate how much a feature depends on genes and how much on the environment.
bullets: Identical twins: **same alleles**, so differences = **environmental**
Non-identical twins: from two eggs and two sperm, so they are no more alike genetically than ordinary brothers and sisters
If identical twins raised apart are still very similar for a feature, that feature is **strongly genetic**
If identical twins raised apart differ a lot, the **environment** has a big effect
Example: identical twins can differ in body mass if they have different diets and exercise, but always share the same blood group

callouts.p: Comment on sample size, and note that twins raised apart may still share some environment (the same uterus before birth).

core.p: Because of mutation and sexual reproduction, a population usually contains **extensive genetic variation**: many genes have several alleles in the population. This matters for survival of the species.
bullets: Different alleles give different phenotypes, so individuals differ in how well they survive and reproduce
If the environment changes, some individuals are likely to have alleles that help them survive: the basis of **natural selection**
Populations with **low genetic variation** (for example clones, or very small populations) are more at risk from new diseases or climate change
The **Human Genome Project** has shown that humans share most of their DNA but differ at many individual bases

core.p: You may be asked to plan or interpret an investigation of variation, such as measuring the hand span or height of students, or the length of leaves from a plant.
bullets: Measure a **large sample** (for example 30 or more) chosen **at random** to make results representative
Use suitable equipment, for example a **ruler or tape measure** in mm or cm
Group continuous data into **class intervals** and plot a **histogram**
Calculate the **mean**, and if needed the **range**
To study environmental effects, keep **genotype the same** (for example clones or cuttings of one plant) and change **one environmental factor**, such as light intensity
To study genetic effects, keep the **environment the same** and compare different varieties

callouts.t: Use clones to test the environment
callouts.p: Cuttings from one plant are genetically identical, so any differences when grown in different light must be environmental.

analogy.p: Your genome is like a recipe book for a cake, and most features, like height, are not set by one line of the recipe but by many ingredients (genes) each adding a little: more flour, more sugar, more eggs. Small differences in lots of ingredients give a smooth range of cake sizes rather than just 'big' or 'small'. Mutation is like a misprint that creates a new version of an instruction, and sexual reproduction is like mixing half the recipe from one book with half from another. The environment is the cook and the oven: the same recipe baked in a cold oven or with too little batter will not reach its full size. Where it breaks down: a recipe is followed once, but genes are expressed throughout life in response to the environment, and a cook can deliberately change a cake, whereas environmental effects on organisms are not chosen and are not passed on.

terms.d: Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species.
The observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from its genotype and its environment.
The combination of alleles an organism has.
Controlled by several (multiple) genes rather than one gene.
When a characteristic is controlled by one gene, as in a monohybrid cross.
Different characteristics as a result of mutation or sexual reproduction (differences in alleles).
Different characteristics caused by an organism's interaction with the environment.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA, which may produce a new allele.
A different form of the same gene.
Reproduction involving the fusion of two gametes from two parents, producing genetically different offspring.
Cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes.
The chance fusion of any one male gamete with any one female gamete.
Variation in which a characteristic can take any value within a range, such as height.
Variation in which individuals fall into distinct categories, such as blood group.
A symmetrical bell-shaped spread of data with most individuals close to the mean.
Twins formed from one fertilised egg that splits, so they have identical genotypes.

mistakes.w: Most characteristics are controlled by a single gene.
mistakes.r: Most phenotypic features are the result of multiple genes rather than single gene inheritance.

mistakes.w: Sexual reproduction creates new alleles.
mistakes.r: Mutation creates new alleles; sexual reproduction (meiosis and random fertilisation) produces new combinations of alleles.

mistakes.w: Height is genetic.
mistakes.r: Height is affected by many genes and by environmental factors such as diet, so it is caused by both.

mistakes.w: A scar or large muscles from training can be inherited.
mistakes.r: Environmental changes do not alter the DNA in gametes, so they are not inherited.

mistakes.w: Identical twins have different phenotypes because of different genes.
mistakes.r: Identical twins have identical genotypes, so differences between them are caused by the environment.

mistakes.w: All mutations are harmful.
mistakes.r: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype; some are harmful and a few are beneficial.

mistakes.w: Plotting continuous data such as height on a bar chart with gaps.
mistakes.r: Continuous data is grouped into class intervals and plotted as a histogram with no gaps.

mistakes.w: Environmental variation is variation caused by the weather.
mistakes.r: Environmental variation is caused by any interaction with the environment, including diet, light, minerals, disease and lifestyle.

exam.q: State how most phenotypic features are inherited.
model: They are controlled by multiple genes (rather than a single gene)
exam.tip: Use the word 'multiple' or 'many' genes.

exam.q: Give two causes of genetic variation.
model: Mutation
Sexual reproduction (accept meiosis / random fertilisation)
exam.tip: These are the two the spec names.

exam.q: Give one example of a human characteristic caused only by the environment.
model: Scar / language spoken / accent / tattoo / pierced ears (any one)
exam.tip: Avoid height or body mass: they are caused by both.

exam.q: Explain why human height shows continuous variation.
model: Height is controlled by many genes
Each gene has a small additive effect, giving many possible combinations/intermediate values
Environmental factors such as diet also affect height, so it can take any value in a range
exam.tip: Mention both genes and environment for full marks.

exam.q: Explain how mutation leads to genetic variation.
model: A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence
This produces a new allele (which may change the phenotype and be passed on in gametes)
exam.tip: Link base sequence to new allele.

exam.q: Explain how sexual reproduction produces genetic variation in offspring.
model: Meiosis produces genetically different gametes
Fertilisation is random, so any gamete can fuse with any other
Offspring receive a combination of alleles from two parents / new combinations of alleles
exam.tip: Sexual reproduction makes new combinations, not new alleles.

exam.q: Identical twins were separated at birth. At age 30 one twin weighed 68 kg and the other weighed 81 kg. Both were blood group A. Explain these observations.
model: Identical twins have identical genotypes/alleles
Blood group is controlled by genes only, so they have the same blood group
Body mass is affected by the environment (and many genes)
Different diets/exercise/lifestyles explain the difference in body mass
exam.tip: Use the data: quote the 13 kg difference.

exam.q: A student grew cuttings from one plant in different light intensities. The plants in bright light were shorter with smaller leaves. Explain why the student used cuttings from one plant.
model: Cuttings are clones / genetically identical
So any differences must be caused by the environment (light intensity), not genes
exam.tip: This is about controlling the genetic variable.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate variation in hand span in their year group and present the results.
model: Measure hand span of a large random sample (e.g. at least 30 students)
Use a ruler, measuring from thumb tip to little finger tip, in mm
Group the data into class intervals and record frequency in a table
Plot a histogram (no gaps) and describe the distribution / calculate the mean
exam.tip: Continuous data means a histogram.

exam.q: Discuss the causes of variation in the phenotypes of individuals within a species. Use examples in your answer.
model: Phenotype results from genotype and the environment
Genetic variation is caused by mutation, which changes the DNA base sequence and creates new alleles
Genetic variation is also caused by sexual reproduction: meiosis gives genetically different gametes and fertilisation is random, giving new combinations of alleles
Most features are controlled by multiple genes, giving continuous variation, e.g. height or skin colour; a few are single gene, e.g. blood group
Environmental variation is caused by interaction with the environment, e.g. diet, sunlight, light intensity or minerals for plants, scars or language in humans
Most features result from both, e.g. genes set potential height and diet determines whether it is reached; environmental changes are not inherited
exam.tip: Structure: genetic causes, then environmental causes, then both, with an example for each.

worked.q: A feature is controlled by two genes, A and B. Each contributing allele (A or B) adds 5 cm to a plant's base height of 20 cm. What is the range of possible heights, and what height is most common in the offspring of AaBb x AaBb?
steps: The number of contributing alleles can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4
Heights: 20 + (0 x 5) = 20 cm up to 20 + (4 x 5) = 40 cm
The offspring ratio of 0 : 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 contributing alleles is 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1
The most common class has 2 contributing alleles: 20 + 10 = 30 cm
This shows that even two genes give a peaked, bell-like distribution
worked.ans: Heights range from 20 cm to 40 cm; 30 cm is the most common (6 out of 16 = 37.5%)

worked.q: Classify each of the following as caused by genes, the environment, or both, and explain one: ABO blood group, accent, body mass, skin colour.
steps: ABO blood group: genes only (a single gene with three alleles, not changed by surroundings)
Accent: environment only (learned from the people around you)
Body mass: both (many genes affect metabolism and appetite; diet and exercise change mass)
Skin colour: both (many genes control melanin; sunlight causes tanning)
Example explanation: identical twins always share a blood group but can differ in body mass if their diets differ
worked.ans: Genes: blood group; environment: accent; both: body mass and skin colour

bio_edx.2.3.summary: DNA can be extracted from fruit such as **strawberries or kiwi fruit** using simple kitchen-style chemicals. The fruit is **mashed** to break cell walls, **detergent** breaks down the **cell and nuclear membranes** to release the DNA, **salt** makes the DNA strands clump together, and filtering removes cell debris. Finally **ice-cold ethanol** is poured gently on top, and because DNA is **insoluble in cold ethanol** it **precipitates** as white, stringy strands at the boundary, which can be lifted out with a glass rod.

core.h: Why we extract DNA from fruit
core.p: This practical shows that DNA is a real, physical substance found in the **nucleus of every cell**. Fruit is used because it is soft, cheap and safe, and because many cultivated fruits are **polyploid**, meaning each cell has many copies of each chromosome, so a lot of DNA is released.
bullets: **Strawberries** are octoploid (8 sets of chromosomes) so give a large, visible amount of DNA.
**Kiwi fruit**, bananas and onions are also commonly used.
Fruit is soft, so it is easy to break open the cells by mashing.
The DNA from millions of cells clumps together, so we can see it with the naked eye even though one DNA molecule is far too thin to see.
No microscope is needed to see the final product.

callouts.p: In plant cells the DNA is inside the **nucleus**, surrounded by the **nuclear membrane**, inside the **cell membrane**, inside the **cell wall**. The method must get through all of these barriers.

core.p: You need simple apparatus, but each chemical has a specific job that you must be able to explain.
bullets: Fruit (for example strawberries or kiwi fruit).
Pestle and mortar, or a sealable plastic bag, to **mash** the fruit.
**Extraction solution**: **washing-up liquid (detergent)** + **table salt (sodium chloride)** + distilled water.
Water bath at about **60 degrees C**, and an ice bath.
Funnel and **filter paper** (or muslin / coffee filter) and a beaker or boiling tube.
Optional: **protease enzyme** (for example from fresh pineapple juice or contact lens cleaner).
**Ice-cold ethanol** (kept in a freezer or on ice).
Glass rod or wooden splint to **spool** (wind up) the DNA.

head: Chemical
Job
rows: Breaks down lipids in cell and nuclear membranes, releasing DNA
Makes DNA strands clump together (so they come out of solution)
Breaks down proteins, including histones bound to DNA
DNA is insoluble in it, so DNA precipitates out

core.p: The fruit is first **mashed** (in a pestle and mortar or squeezed in a plastic bag) with the extraction solution.
bullets: Mashing **breaks down the cell walls** and separates the cells.
It greatly **increases the surface area** of the cells exposed to the detergent and salt.
This means more cells release their DNA, so the yield is higher.
Mash gently enough to avoid making large amounts of froth from the detergent.
Do not grind for too long or too hard, as very vigorous mixing can **break the long DNA strands into small fragments**.

callouts.p: Write: mashing **breaks cell walls** and **increases surface area** for the detergent to act on.

core.p: **Detergent** (washing-up liquid) is the key chemical for releasing DNA. Cell membranes and the nuclear membrane are made mainly of **lipids (phospholipids)**, and detergent breaks down (emulsifies) lipids in the same way it removes grease from plates.
bullets: Detergent **breaks down the cell membrane** so the contents of the cell are released.
Detergent **breaks down the nuclear membrane** so the **DNA is released** from the nucleus.
Detergent cannot break the cellulose **cell wall**, which is why mashing is also needed.
The DNA is now free in solution with proteins, sugars and other cell contents.

callouts.p: Detergent breaks down the **lipids** in the **cell membrane and nuclear membrane**, releasing DNA.

fig.cap: Releasing the DNA: mashing breaks the cellulose cell wall, then detergent breaks down the lipid cell membrane and nuclear membrane so the DNA spills out into the solution.

core.h: Step 3: Salt makes the DNA clump
core.p: **Salt** (sodium chloride) is added in the extraction solution. DNA molecules have a **negative charge** along their backbone, which makes the strands repel each other and stay dissolved.
bullets: The positive sodium ions from salt **neutralise the negative charges** on DNA.
This lets the DNA strands **clump (aggregate) together** instead of repelling each other.
Clumped DNA comes out of solution more easily when ethanol is added, so it is visible.
Salt also helps separate proteins from the DNA.
At GCSE, the mark-scheme phrase is that salt makes the **DNA clump together**.

callouts.p: Salt does **not** break down membranes; that is the detergent's job. Salt causes the **DNA to clump**.

core.h: Step 4: Warming in a water bath
core.p: The mixture is placed in a **water bath at about 60 degrees C for about 15 minutes**, then cooled quickly in an ice bath.
bullets: Warming speeds up the action of the detergent on the membranes.
The heat **denatures enzymes** in the cell (DNases) that would otherwise **break down (digest) the DNA**.
It also denatures many other cell proteins, helping separate them from DNA.
Do not heat for too long or too hot, as this can start to **break up the DNA** itself.
Cooling in an **ice bath** afterwards slows any remaining enzyme activity and protects the DNA.

core.p: The mixture is poured through **filter paper** (or muslin) in a funnel into a clean boiling tube or beaker.
bullets: Filtering **removes the cell debris**: cell wall fragments, seeds, unbroken cells and other insoluble material.
The **filtrate** (liquid that passes through) contains the dissolved **DNA**.
Collect only a small volume of filtrate (for example a few cm3 in a test tube) so the ethanol layer is easy to add.
Do not squeeze the filter paper hard, or debris will be pushed through.

callouts.p: The liquid that passes through the filter paper; here it contains the DNA.

core.p: In the nucleus, DNA is wrapped around proteins called **histones**. A few drops of a **protease** enzyme can be added to the filtrate to break these down.
bullets: **Protease** breaks down proteins (into amino acids).
This frees the DNA from the histone proteins and other proteins, giving purer DNA.
Sources: fresh **pineapple juice** (contains the protease bromelain) or **contact lens cleaning solution**.
Must be added **after** heating, otherwise the heat would denature the protease enzyme.

callouts.p: If asked why protease is added after the water bath, say the high temperature would **denature** the enzyme so it would no longer work.

core.p: The final, most important step. **Ice-cold ethanol** is poured **slowly and carefully down the side** of the tilted tube so that it forms a **separate layer on top** of the filtrate, without mixing.
bullets: DNA is **soluble in water** but **insoluble in cold ethanol**.
Where the two layers meet, the DNA **precipitates** (comes out of solution) as **white, stringy, cloudy strands**.
The ethanol is less dense than the filtrate, so it floats on top as a layer.
The ethanol is **ice-cold** because DNA is **even less soluble at low temperature**, so more precipitates; cold also slows enzymes that could break down DNA.
Leave the tube **still** for a few minutes; shaking would mix the layers and break up the strands.
The DNA rises up into the ethanol layer.

callouts.p: DNA is **insoluble in ice-cold ethanol**, so it **precipitates** at the boundary between the filtrate and the ethanol layer.

fig.cap: The final tube: ice-cold ethanol floats as a layer on top of the filtrate. DNA precipitates as white strands where the layers meet and can be spooled onto a glass rod.

core.h: Step 7: Spooling and observing the DNA
core.p: The DNA can be collected by gently **twisting a glass rod or wooden splint** at the boundary between the layers. The long DNA fibres wrap around the rod (this is called **spooling**).
bullets: Extracted DNA looks like **white, stringy, slimy fibres** or a cloudy precipitate.
What you see is millions of DNA molecules clumped together, **not** a single molecule and **not** visible double helices.
It is not pure: it still contains some RNA and protein.
The DNA can be placed in a small tube of ethanol and kept.

callouts.t: What you can and cannot see
callouts.p: You **cannot** see the double helix or individual genes with the naked eye; you see a **mass of DNA strands clumped together**.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to put the steps in order or to write the method as a 6-mark answer. Learn the sequence and the reason for each step.
bullets: Every step has a reason linked to getting through a barrier (wall, membrane) or getting DNA out of solution.
Ice-cold ethanol always comes **last**, after filtering.

head: Order
Step
Reason
rows: Breaks cell walls, increases surface area
Detergent breaks membranes; salt clumps DNA
Denatures enzymes that would digest DNA
Removes cell debris; filtrate contains DNA
Breaks down proteins such as histones
DNA insoluble in cold ethanol, precipitates

core.h: Safety, errors and improving the yield
core.p: As with any practical, you may be asked about risks and how to get better results.
bullets: **Ethanol is highly flammable**: keep away from naked flames (no Bunsen burners).
Ethanol is an irritant: wear **eye protection**; ice-cold ethanol should be handled carefully.
Take care with hot water baths and glassware.
Do not eat the fruit or taste any solutions in the lab.
Little or no DNA? Possible causes: ethanol not cold enough, layers mixed by pouring too fast or shaking, too little mashing, too little detergent, or overheating which broke up the DNA.
To increase yield: use more fruit, mash thoroughly, use colder ethanol, pour slowly to keep a clear layer, and leave for longer before spooling.

callouts.p: For risk questions give the **hazard** (ethanol is flammable) **and** the **precaution** (keep away from flames).

analogy.t: Getting the treasure out of a locked safe in a locked room
analogy.p: The DNA is like **treasure in a safe (nucleus) inside a room (cell membrane) inside a building (cell wall)**. Mashing **knocks down the building walls**. Detergent is a **chemical key** that dissolves the fatty locks on the room and the safe, so the treasure spills out. Salt is like **putting the loose coins into bags** so they stick together. Filtering **sweeps away the rubble**. Finally ice-cold ethanol is like a **magnet** layer that the treasure cannot stay dissolved beneath, so it rises up and can be scooped out with a rod. Where it breaks down: ethanol does not attract DNA; DNA simply **cannot stay dissolved** in cold ethanol so it precipitates, and the 'treasure' you collect is a tangled mass of millions of molecules, not neat individual items.

terms.d: Deoxyribonucleic acid: the polymer that carries the genetic code, found in the nucleus of plant and animal cells.
The organelle that contains the cell's genetic material (DNA) arranged as chromosomes.
The partially permeable layer made of lipids and proteins that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell.
The double membrane made of lipids and proteins that surrounds the nucleus.
A rigid layer made of cellulose outside the cell membrane of plant cells.
A chemical (such as washing-up liquid) that breaks down lipids, so it breaks down the cell and nuclear membranes.
A fat or oil molecule; phospholipids form the main structure of cell membranes.
Added to the extraction solution to make DNA strands clump together.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids; used to remove proteins such as histones from DNA.
Proteins around which DNA is wrapped in the nucleus.
To change the shape of an enzyme's active site, for example by high temperature, so it no longer works.
The liquid that passes through filter paper; here it contains dissolved DNA.
An alcohol in which DNA is insoluble when ice-cold, used to precipitate DNA; it is highly flammable.
To come out of solution as a solid; DNA precipitates as white strands in cold ethanol.
Winding the precipitated DNA strands onto a glass rod to collect them.
Having more than two sets of chromosomes in each cell, as in strawberries, so there is more DNA to extract.

mistakes.w: Detergent breaks down the cell wall.
mistakes.r: Detergent breaks down the **lipids in the cell membrane and nuclear membrane**; mashing breaks the cell wall.

mistakes.w: Salt breaks open the cells.
mistakes.r: Salt makes the **DNA clump together** (so it can precipitate).

mistakes.w: Ethanol dissolves the DNA.
mistakes.r: DNA is **insoluble** in cold ethanol, so it **precipitates** out.

mistakes.w: The ethanol is cold to keep it safe.
mistakes.r: Ice-cold ethanol makes DNA **less soluble** so more precipitates (and slows enzymes that break down DNA).

mistakes.w: You can see the double helix in the tube.
mistakes.r: You see **white strands made of millions of DNA molecules clumped together**, not a double helix.

mistakes.w: Heat the mixture to boiling.
mistakes.r: Use a water bath at about **60 degrees C** to denature enzymes; too hot or too long breaks up the DNA.

mistakes.w: Shake the tube after adding ethanol.
mistakes.r: Pour ethanol **slowly down the side** to form a **separate layer** and do not shake.

mistakes.w: The DNA is in the filter paper.
mistakes.r: The DNA is in the **filtrate**; the filter paper holds back the cell debris.

mistakes.w: Protease is added to break down the DNA.
mistakes.r: Protease breaks down **proteins** (such as histones), freeing the DNA.

exam.q: Give the reason for adding detergent when extracting DNA from fruit.
model: To break down the (lipids in the) cell membrane / nuclear membrane (to release DNA).
exam.tip: Mention membranes, not cell walls.

exam.q: State why the fruit is mashed.
model: To break down the cell walls / increase surface area (for the detergent).
exam.tip: One clear reason is enough for 1 mark.

exam.q: State the appearance of DNA when it has been extracted.
model: White / colourless strands / threads / fibres / cloudy precipitate.
exam.tip: Strands or threads is the expected word.

exam.q: Give one safety precaution when using ethanol in this experiment.
model: Keep away from naked flames because it is (highly) flammable / wear eye protection.
exam.tip: Link the precaution to the hazard.

exam.q: Explain why salt is added to the extraction solution.
model: Salt causes the DNA (strands) to clump together.
So it comes out of solution / precipitates and is visible / can be collected.
exam.tip: Second mark: why clumping helps.

exam.q: Explain why the ethanol must be ice-cold and poured slowly down the side of the tube.
model: DNA is insoluble in (cold) ethanol so it precipitates.
Cold ethanol increases the amount of DNA that precipitates / slows enzymes that break down DNA.
Pouring slowly makes a separate layer on top of the filtrate (so DNA forms at the boundary and is not broken up).
exam.tip: Two ideas: the temperature and the layer.

exam.q: Explain why the mixture is placed in a water bath at 60 degrees C, and why it should not be left there for too long.
model: The heat denatures enzymes that would break down / digest the DNA.
Too long / too hot would break down the DNA itself.
exam.tip: Use the word 'denature' for enzymes.

exam.q: A student added protease to the filtrate before putting it in the 60 degrees C water bath. Explain why this was a mistake.
model: Protease is an enzyme that breaks down proteins (histones) around the DNA.
The high temperature would denature the protease so it would not work.
exam.tip: Link to enzyme denaturation.

exam.q: A student obtained very little DNA. Suggest three reasons why.
model: Ethanol was not cold enough.
The ethanol was poured too fast / tube was shaken so the layers mixed.
Fruit not mashed enough / too little detergent so few cells broken open.
Mixture overheated / heated too long so DNA broke up (any three).
exam.tip: Each reason should link to a specific step.

exam.q: Describe a method to extract DNA from strawberries. Give reasons for each step.
model: Mash the strawberries to break the cell walls / increase surface area.
Add a solution of detergent and salt.
Detergent breaks down the cell membrane and nuclear membrane releasing DNA.
Salt makes the DNA clump together.
Place in a water bath at about 60 degrees C for about 15 minutes to denature enzymes that digest DNA, then cool.
Filter to remove cell debris; collect the filtrate.
Pour ice-cold ethanol slowly down the side of the tube to form a layer.
DNA is insoluble in cold ethanol so it precipitates as white strands at the boundary; collect with a glass rod.
exam.tip: A Level 3 answer gives steps in a logical order with a reason for each step.

worked.q: Put these steps in the correct order and give the purpose of each: filter the mixture; add ice-cold ethanol; mash the fruit with detergent and salt; place in a 60 degrees C water bath.
steps: 1st: **mash the fruit with detergent and salt**. Mashing breaks cell walls; detergent breaks the cell and nuclear membranes; salt clumps the DNA.
2nd: **water bath at 60 degrees C**. Denatures enzymes that would digest the DNA.
3rd: **filter the mixture**. Removes cell debris; the filtrate contains the DNA.
4th: **add ice-cold ethanol** slowly down the side of the tube. DNA is insoluble in cold ethanol so it precipitates at the boundary.
worked.ans: Mash with detergent and salt, water bath, filter, then add ice-cold ethanol.

worked.q: A class compares DNA extraction from strawberries and kiwi fruit. Strawberries give a much larger mass of DNA from the same mass of fruit. Suggest a reason, and describe how to make the comparison fair.
steps: Strawberries are **polyploid** (8 sets of chromosomes), so each cell contains more DNA; they are also very soft so more cells break open.
Fair test: use the **same mass of fruit** each time.
Use the **same volume and concentration** of detergent and salt solution.
Use the **same water bath temperature and time**, the same volume of **ice-cold ethanol** at the same temperature, and the same time before spooling.
Measure DNA in the same way, for example the mass of DNA on the rod after drying, and repeat to calculate a mean.
worked.ans: Strawberry cells contain more copies of chromosomes (polyploid), so more DNA per gram; control fruit mass, solution volumes, temperatures and times, and repeat.

bio_edx.2.4.summary: The **order of bases** in a gene is a code for the **order of amino acids** in a protein, and that order decides how the protein **folds** into its specific shape and so how it works. Protein synthesis has two stages: in **transcription** (in the nucleus) **RNA polymerase** binds to **non-coding DNA in front of a gene** and makes a complementary **mRNA** copy of the gene; in **translation** (in the cytoplasm) the mRNA attaches to a **ribosome**, where each **triplet of bases (codon)** is matched by a **tRNA** carrying a specific **amino acid**. The amino acids are joined together to form a **polypeptide**, which folds into a protein.

core.p: A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for a specific **protein**. DNA is made of nucleotides, each with one of four bases: **A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine) and G (guanine)**. The sequence of these bases is the instruction for building the protein.
bullets: Proteins are **polymers** made of **amino acids** joined in a chain (a **polypeptide**).
There are about **20 different amino acids**.
Each **sequence of three bases (a triplet)** codes for **one specific amino acid**.
So the **order of bases** in a gene determines the **order of amino acids** in the protein.
Proteins are made in the cytoplasm on **ribosomes**, but DNA stays in the **nucleus**, so a messenger molecule (mRNA) is needed to carry the code.

callouts.p: The order of bases in a gene; each sequence of three bases (triplet) codes for a specific amino acid.

core.h: From base sequence to protein shape and function
core.p: The order of amino acids decides how the polypeptide **folds**. Different amino acids interact with each other in different ways, so the chain folds into a **specific 3D shape**, and the shape decides the protein's function.
bullets: Base sequence of gene -> amino acid sequence -> folding -> **specific shape** -> **function**.
Example: an **enzyme** has an **active site** with a specific shape that is **complementary to its substrate**.
Other examples: haemoglobin (carries oxygen), antibodies (bind to specific antigens), hormones such as insulin, structural proteins such as collagen and keratin.

If the base sequence changes (a mutation), the amino acid sequence may change, so the protein may fold differently and may **not function** (for example the active site may no longer fit the substrate).

callouts.p: Change in base sequence -> change in amino acid sequence -> change in **folding / shape** -> change in **function**. Use every link in the chain for full marks.

core.p: Protein synthesis uses **RNA** as well as DNA. You must know how they differ, especially the base **uracil**.
bullets: **mRNA (messenger RNA)** is a single-stranded copy of a gene that carries the code from the nucleus to the ribosome.
**tRNA (transfer RNA)** carries specific amino acids to the ribosome.
In RNA, **uracil (U)** replaces thymine (T), so A pairs with **U**.
mRNA is much **shorter** than DNA (a copy of one gene only), so it is small enough to leave the nucleus through **nuclear pores**.

head: Feature
DNA
mRNA
rows: Made in nucleus, moves to cytoplasm

callouts.p: Never write thymine in an mRNA sequence. In mRNA the base complementary to A is **U (uracil)**.

core.p: **Transcription** is the first stage of protein synthesis. It takes place in the **nucleus** and makes an **mRNA** copy of a gene. It is needed because DNA is too large to leave the nucleus, but ribosomes are in the cytoplasm.
bullets: Only the gene being expressed is copied, not the whole chromosome.
The mRNA is **complementary** to the DNA template strand.
Many mRNA copies can be made from one gene, so lots of protein can be made quickly.
The DNA itself is not used up or changed.

callouts.p: The process in the nucleus in which RNA polymerase makes a complementary mRNA copy of a gene from the DNA.

core.p: Learn these steps in order, using the exact words the mark scheme rewards.
bullets: 1. **RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA located in front of the gene** (this region is called the **promoter**).
2. The two DNA strands **unzip**: hydrogen bonds between complementary bases break, exposing the bases.
3. RNA polymerase moves along the **coding DNA** of the gene, using one strand as a **template**.
4. Free RNA nucleotides line up by **complementary base pairing**: A-U, T-A, C-G, G-C.
5. RNA polymerase **joins the nucleotides together** to form a strand of **mRNA**.
6. At the end of the gene the mRNA detaches; the DNA strands rejoin.
7. The mRNA **leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore** and travels to a ribosome in the cytoplasm.

callouts.p: The **non-coding DNA in front of a gene** is where **RNA polymerase binds**. It does not code for amino acids, but it controls whether the gene is transcribed.

core.p: **Translation** is the second stage. It takes place on **ribosomes in the cytoplasm**. The base sequence of mRNA is 'translated' into a sequence of amino acids.
bullets: The mRNA **attaches to a ribosome**.
The ribosome reads the mRNA **three bases at a time**; each triplet on mRNA is called a **codon**.
Each codon codes for **one specific amino acid**.
**tRNA** molecules bring the correct amino acids to the ribosome.
Each tRNA has an **anticodon** (three bases) at one end and carries **one specific amino acid** at the other.

callouts.p: The process on a ribosome in which the codons on mRNA are read and tRNA brings the matching amino acids, which are joined to form a polypeptide.

core.p: Learn these in order.
bullets: 1. The **mRNA attaches to a ribosome** in the cytoplasm.
2. The ribosome reads the first **codon** (triplet of bases) on the mRNA.
3. A **tRNA** with the **complementary anticodon** pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing, bringing its **specific amino acid**.
4. The ribosome moves along to the next codon and another tRNA brings the next amino acid.
5. The ribosome **joins the adjacent amino acids together** (by a peptide bond), forming a chain.
6. The empty tRNA leaves to collect another amino acid of the same type from the cytoplasm.
7. This continues until a **stop codon** is reached; the finished **polypeptide** is released.
8. The polypeptide **folds** into its specific 3D shape to become a functional **protein**.

callouts.p: **Codon** = triplet on **mRNA**. **Anticodon** = complementary triplet on **tRNA**. Mixing these up is a very common mark loss.

core.h: Complementary base pairing all the way through
core.p: The whole of protein synthesis depends on **complementary base pairing**. Questions often give you one sequence and ask you to work out another.
bullets: DNA template to mRNA: A->U, T->A, C->G, G->C.
mRNA codon to tRNA anticodon: A->U, U->A, C->G, G->C.
So the tRNA anticodon has the **same sequence as the DNA template strand**, except with U in place of T.
Number of amino acids = number of bases in coding sequence / 3 (ignoring the stop codon).
Number of bases needed = number of amino acids x 3.

callouts.p: Always split sequences into **triplets** first; count codons, not bases, when working out amino acids.

core.p: Being able to give a clear overview of the whole process gets you marks in 6-mark questions.
bullets: Nucleus: DNA -> (transcription by RNA polymerase) -> mRNA.
mRNA leaves via a nuclear pore.
Cytoplasm: mRNA + ribosome + tRNA + amino acids -> (translation) -> polypeptide.
Polypeptide folds -> protein with specific shape and function.
