core.h: Why the system works this way
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain the **reasons** behind each feature, not just the steps.
bullets: DNA stays in the nucleus where it is **protected** from damage; only short mRNA copies go to the cytoplasm.
Using an mRNA copy means the gene can be read **many times** to make lots of protein.
A **triplet** code is needed because with 4 bases, pairs would give only 4 x 4 = 16 combinations, too few for 20 amino acids; triplets give 4 x 4 x 4 = **64**, enough.
Because there are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, **some amino acids are coded by more than one codon**; some codons are **stop** signals.
Complementary base pairing ensures the code is copied and read **accurately**.

callouts.p: 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 possible triplets, which is more than the 20 amino acids needed.

core.p: This point underpins the next spec points on genetic variants. You may need to explain how a change in DNA affects a protein using transcription and translation.
bullets: A change in the **coding DNA** changes the mRNA codon, which may code for a **different amino acid**, changing the polypeptide's folding and **shape** (for example an enzyme's active site), so the protein may not work.
A change in the **non-coding DNA in front of a gene** may affect how well **RNA polymerase binds**, so **more or less mRNA is transcribed** and more or less protein is made.
Some base changes have **no effect** because the new codon codes for the **same amino acid**.

callouts.p: When explaining effects, always go through: DNA -> mRNA -> amino acid -> shape -> function.

analogy.t: A library recipe book and a kitchen
analogy.p: The **DNA is a precious recipe book in a reference library (nucleus)** that cannot be taken out. **Transcription** is like the librarian (**RNA polymerase**) finding the right page by its title heading (**non-coding DNA in front of the gene**) and **photocopying one recipe** (mRNA). The photocopy is taken to the **kitchen (cytoplasm)**, where the **chef (ribosome)** reads it **three letters at a time**. Each three-letter word asks for one ingredient, and **kitchen porters (tRNA)** each bring one specific ingredient (amino acid) and can only respond to their own word (anticodon matching codon). The chef joins the ingredients in order to make the dish (polypeptide), which is then shaped (folded) before it is served. Where it breaks down: a real recipe allows ingredients in any order with any spacing, whereas the genetic code has no gaps and the exact order of every amino acid matters; also the photocopy here is complementary to the original, not identical to it.

terms.d: A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.
The sequence of bases in DNA, read in triplets, each triplet coding for a specific amino acid.
A sequence of three bases in DNA that codes for one amino acid.
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one specific amino acid.
A sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to a codon on mRNA.
The monomer (building block) of proteins; there are about 20 types.
A chain of amino acids joined together; one or more polypeptides fold to form a protein.
The making of a complementary mRNA copy of a gene by RNA polymerase in the nucleus.
The process on ribosomes where the mRNA code is used to join amino acids, brought by tRNA, into a polypeptide.
The enzyme that binds to non-coding DNA in front of a gene and joins RNA nucleotides to make mRNA.
The region of non-coding DNA in front of a gene where RNA polymerase binds.
Messenger RNA: a single-stranded copy of a gene that carries the code from the nucleus to a ribosome.
Transfer RNA: a molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and has an anticodon.
The organelle in the cytoplasm where translation (protein synthesis) takes place.
The base found in RNA instead of thymine; it pairs with adenine.
The pairing of specific bases: A with T (or U in RNA) and C with G.
DNA that does not code for amino acids; some of it, in front of a gene, is where RNA polymerase binds.

mistakes.w: Each base codes for one amino acid.
mistakes.r: Each **sequence of three bases (triplet / codon)** codes for one amino acid.

mistakes.w: Transcription happens on the ribosome.
mistakes.r: Transcription happens in the **nucleus**; translation happens on **ribosomes in the cytoplasm**.

mistakes.w: DNA leaves the nucleus and goes to the ribosome.
mistakes.r: DNA stays in the nucleus; **mRNA** leaves through a nuclear pore.

mistakes.w: The mRNA sequence complementary to A on DNA is T.
mistakes.r: In mRNA, **U (uracil)** pairs with A; RNA has no thymine.

mistakes.w: DNA polymerase makes mRNA.
mistakes.r: **RNA polymerase** makes mRNA.

mistakes.w: RNA polymerase binds to the gene / to the start of the coding DNA.
mistakes.r: RNA polymerase binds to **non-coding DNA located in front of the gene**.

mistakes.w: tRNA carries the code from the nucleus.
mistakes.r: **mRNA** carries the code; **tRNA** carries **amino acids** to the ribosome.

mistakes.w: The anticodon is on the mRNA.
mistakes.r: **Codons** are on mRNA; **anticodons** are on tRNA.

mistakes.w: The ribosome makes amino acids.
mistakes.r: The ribosome **joins** amino acids together; the amino acids are already in the cytoplasm and are brought by tRNA.

exam.q: Name the enzyme that makes mRNA during transcription.
model: RNA polymerase.
exam.tip: Not DNA polymerase.

exam.q: State where in a cell translation takes place.
model: On ribosomes / in the cytoplasm.
exam.tip: Ribosome is the best answer.

exam.q: State the number of bases that code for one amino acid.
model: Three / a triplet.
exam.tip: Say three, not 'a few'.

exam.q: Give the mRNA sequence produced from the DNA template strand TACGGA.
model: AUGCCU.
exam.tip: Replace T with U in RNA.

exam.q: Describe the role of tRNA in protein synthesis.
model: Carries / transfers a specific amino acid to the ribosome.
Its anticodon pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA (so amino acids are in the correct order).
exam.tip: Mention both the amino acid and the anticodon.

exam.q: Explain why mRNA is needed in protein synthesis.
model: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus / stays in the nucleus.
mRNA carries a copy of the gene / code out of the nucleus (through nuclear pores) to the ribosome in the cytoplasm.
exam.tip: Link the location of DNA to the location of ribosomes.

exam.q: Explain how the order of bases in a gene determines the function of a protein.
model: Each triplet of bases codes for a specific amino acid, so base order determines the order of amino acids.
The order of amino acids determines how the polypeptide folds / its 3D shape.
The shape determines the function, e.g. the shape of an enzyme's active site.
exam.tip: Follow every link of the chain.

exam.q: A section of mRNA is 360 bases long, not including the stop codon. Calculate the number of amino acids in the polypeptide.
model: = 120 amino acids.
exam.tip: Divide by 3 for codons.

exam.q: Describe the process of transcription.
model: RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA in front of the gene.
DNA strands separate / unzip.
Complementary (free RNA) nucleotides pair with bases on the template strand; uracil pairs with adenine.
RNA polymerase joins nucleotides to form mRNA.
mRNA leaves the nucleus (through a nuclear pore) (any four).
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'non-coding DNA in front of the gene'.

exam.q: Describe how a protein is made from a gene, including transcription and translation.
model: In the nucleus, RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA in front of the gene.
RNA polymerase makes a complementary mRNA copy of the coding DNA (U pairs with A).
mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore and attaches to a ribosome.
The ribosome reads the mRNA in codons / triplets of bases.
tRNA with complementary anticodons bring specific amino acids to the ribosome.
Amino acids are joined together in the order coded by the mRNA to form a polypeptide.
The polypeptide folds into a specific shape to form the protein.
exam.tip: Level 3: both stages, correct locations, correct molecules, logical order.

exam.q: Explain why there must be at least three bases in the code for each amino acid.
model: There are 20 (different) amino acids.
Two bases give only 16 combinations (4 x 4), whereas three give 64 (4 x 4 x 4), enough for all 20.
exam.tip: Show the arithmetic.

worked.q: The DNA template strand of a short gene is TAC AAA GGC CTA. (a) Write the mRNA. (b) Write the tRNA anticodons. (c) How many amino acids are coded for?
steps: Split into triplets: TAC | AAA | GGC | CTA.
(a) mRNA is complementary, with U instead of T: TAC->AUG, AAA->UUU, GGC->CCG, CTA->GAU. So mRNA = **AUG UUU CCG GAU**.
(b) Anticodons are complementary to the codons: AUG->UAC, UUU->AAA, CCG->GGC, GAU->CUA. So anticodons = **UAC AAA GGC CUA** (the DNA template with U for T).
(c) 4 codons, so **4 amino acids** (assuming none are stop codons).
worked.ans: mRNA AUG UUU CCG GAU; anticodons UAC AAA GGC CUA; 4 amino acids.

worked.q: A protein contains 250 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the mRNA that codes for it, including one stop codon.
steps: Each amino acid needs one codon of 3 bases: 250 x 3 = 750 bases.
Add one stop codon: 750 + 3 = 753 bases.
worked.ans: 753 bases (minimum).

worked.q: A mutation in the non-coding DNA in front of a gene for an enzyme stops RNA polymerase binding. Explain the effect on the cell.
steps: RNA polymerase binds to the non-coding DNA in front of the gene to start transcription.
If it cannot bind, the gene is **not transcribed**, so **no mRNA** is made.
Without mRNA, translation cannot happen, so **no enzyme is produced**.
The reaction the enzyme catalyses will not happen (or will be much slower), affecting the phenotype.
worked.ans: No transcription, so no mRNA, so no enzyme is made and its reaction cannot be catalysed.

bio_edx.2.5.summary: A **genetic variant** is a difference in the base sequence of DNA. Edexcel wants you to explain two routes from a variant to a changed phenotype. A variant in **non-coding DNA** (such as the region where **RNA polymerase** binds before a gene) can change how easily RNA polymerase attaches, so it changes **how much protein** is made. A variant in **coding DNA** can change the **sequence of amino acids**, so the protein folds into a different shape and its **activity** changes (for example an enzyme's active site no longer fits its substrate).

core.p: Every gene is a length of DNA made of a sequence of bases (A, T, C and G). A **genetic variant** is a version of the DNA sequence that differs from the usual one, usually because of a **mutation**. Variants are a normal source of difference between individuals. Many have no effect, some have a small effect and a few have a large effect on the **phenotype** (the observable characteristics).
bullets: A variant can be as small as **one base changed** (a substitution), or a base added (insertion) or removed (deletion).
Variants can occur in **coding DNA** (the part of a gene that codes for amino acids) or **non-coding DNA** (DNA that does not code for amino acids).
Where the variant is decides **how** it affects the phenotype: non-coding variants mainly change the **amount** of protein; coding variants mainly change the **structure** of the protein.
Many variants have **no effect** on phenotype, so a change in genotype does not always mean a change in phenotype.

callouts.p: A difference in the sequence of bases in DNA compared with the most common sequence.
The observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from its genotype and the environment.

core.p: Only part of the DNA in a cell codes for proteins. A gene has a **coding region**, where each **triplet of bases** codes for one amino acid, and in front of it a **non-coding region** that does not code for amino acids but controls whether and how often the gene is used. This control region is where **RNA polymerase** binds to start **transcription**. Much of the genome is non-coding.
bullets: **Coding DNA**: the base sequence is read in triplets; each triplet codes for a specific amino acid.
**Non-coding DNA**: not translated into amino acids, but has important jobs such as switching genes on and off.
The non-coding region just before a gene (often called the **promoter**) is the **binding site for RNA polymerase**.
So non-coding DNA affects **whether a gene is expressed and how much**, while coding DNA affects **what the protein is like**.

head: Feature
Non-coding DNA (before a gene)
Coding DNA
rows: Yes, one triplet per amino acid
Where RNA polymerase binds; controls gene expression
Carries the code for the protein's amino acid sequence
Changes how much protein is made
Changes amino acid sequence, so protein shape and activity

callouts.p: Non-coding variant: changes RNA polymerase binding, so changes quantity of protein. Coding variant: changes amino acid sequence, so changes activity of protein.

fig.cap: A gene has a non-coding region (the promoter) where RNA polymerase binds, followed by the coding region whose triplets code for amino acids. Variants in the promoter change the amount of protein; variants in the coding region change the protein's structure.

core.p: To make a protein, the gene must first be **transcribed** into mRNA. The enzyme **RNA polymerase** has to **bind to the non-coding DNA** just in front of the gene before it can move along and copy the coding region into mRNA. The more easily and more often RNA polymerase binds, the more mRNA is made, and the more mRNA there is, the more protein ribosomes can make by **translation**.
bullets: RNA polymerase binds to the non-coding region **because its shape fits a particular base sequence** there.
Once bound, the DNA unwinds and RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides that are complementary to the template strand, making **mRNA**.
More binding events = **more mRNA molecules** = **more protein**.
So the non-coding region acts like a **volume control** for the gene.

callouts.p: Always write RNA polymerase, not DNA polymerase. DNA polymerase copies DNA in replication; RNA polymerase makes mRNA in transcription.

core.h: Variants in non-coding DNA: changing the quantity of protein
core.p: If a variant changes the base sequence of the non-coding region where RNA polymerase binds, RNA polymerase may bind **less easily (or not at all)**, or in some cases **more easily**. This changes the **rate of transcription**, so the cell makes **less or more mRNA**, and therefore **less or more of the protein**. The protein itself is completely normal, because the coding DNA has not changed; only the **amount** is different.
bullets: Variant makes binding **harder** -> less transcription -> less mRNA -> **less protein**.
Variant makes binding **easier** -> more transcription -> more mRNA -> **more protein**.
Variant stops binding completely -> gene **not expressed** -> **no protein** made.
The amino acid sequence is **unchanged**, so any protein that is made works normally.
The phenotype changes because the **amount** of a protein (for example an enzyme or a pigment-making protein) affects the characteristic.

callouts.p: Variant in non-coding DNA -> changes how well RNA polymerase binds -> changes amount of transcription / mRNA -> changes quantity of protein -> changes phenotype.

callouts.t: Do not say the protein changes shape
callouts.p: A variant in non-coding DNA does not change the amino acid sequence. The protein is the same; only how much of it is made changes.

core.h: Why the amount of protein changes the phenotype
core.p: Many characteristics depend on **how much** of a protein is present. If a protein is an enzyme in a pathway that makes a pigment, less enzyme means a slower reaction and less pigment, so a paler colour. If a protein is a hormone or a receptor, less of it means a weaker response. So simply turning a gene's output up or down can change what we see.
bullets: Less of an enzyme -> **slower rate** of the reaction it catalyses -> less product.
No enzyme at all -> the product may not be made -> a characteristic may be **absent** (for example no pigment).
More of a protein -> may give a **stronger** or more obvious characteristic.
Example used in textbooks: a variant in non-coding DNA near the **lactase** gene keeps the gene switched on into adulthood, so some adults keep making lactase and can digest lactose (milk sugar).

callouts.p: For full marks, do not stop at 'less protein'. Say what less protein does, for example 'less enzyme so slower reaction so less product made'.

core.h: Variants in coding DNA: changing the amino acid sequence
core.p: The coding DNA is read in **triplets**, and each triplet codes for one amino acid. If a variant changes a triplet, the mRNA codon made from it changes, and a **different amino acid** may be added during translation. Because a protein's shape depends on its **sequence of amino acids**, a different amino acid can make the chain **fold differently**, giving a protein with a **different shape** and so a **different activity**.
bullets: Changed base -> changed **triplet** -> changed mRNA **codon** -> possibly a **different amino acid**.
Different amino acid sequence -> different **folding** -> different **3D shape** of the protein.
Different shape -> the protein may work **less well, not at all**, or occasionally **better**.
The **amount** of protein made is usually the same; it is the **activity** that changes.

callouts.p: Variant in coding DNA -> changes base triplet -> changes amino acid sequence -> protein folds into a different shape -> changes protein activity -> changes phenotype.

core.h: Why a changed amino acid changes protein activity
core.p: A protein is a chain of amino acids that **folds into a specific 3D shape**, held by bonds between amino acids in the chain. Changing one amino acid can change where these bonds form, so the protein folds differently. For an **enzyme**, the most important part is the **active site**: if its shape changes, the **substrate no longer fits** (it is no longer complementary), so the enzyme catalyses the reaction more slowly or not at all.
bullets: Enzyme: changed **active site** -> substrate does not fit -> fewer **enzyme-substrate complexes** -> lower activity.
Structural protein (for example in haemoglobin or collagen): changed shape -> protein may not do its job properly.
Carrier or channel protein: changed shape -> may no longer transport a substance across a membrane.
Occasionally a change **improves** activity; this is rare but can be an advantage (a source of variation for natural selection).

callouts.p: The region of an enzyme that the substrate binds to; its shape is complementary to the substrate.
Mark schemes reward: the active site changes shape so the substrate is no longer complementary / no longer fits.

core.h: Types of change in coding DNA and how big their effect is
core.p: Not every coding variant has the same effect. The genetic code is **degenerate**, meaning several triplets can code for the same amino acid, so some substitutions change nothing. Others swap one amino acid, and insertions or deletions can shift the whole reading frame, changing every amino acid after the variant.
bullets: **Substitution** with the same amino acid coded: no change to the protein, **no effect** on phenotype (a silent change).
**Substitution** coding a different amino acid: one amino acid changed; effect can be **none, small or large** depending on where it is.
Substitution that creates a **stop triplet** early: protein is **shorter** and usually does not work.
**Insertion or deletion** of a base: every triplet after it is read differently (a **frameshift**), so many amino acids change and the protein usually **does not work**.

head: Change in coding DNA
Effect on amino acids
Likely effect on protein
rows: None, small or large change in activity
Insertion or deletion of one base
All amino acids after it may change

callouts.p: Do not say every variant causes a disease. Most variants have no or very little effect on phenotype.

core.p: Both kinds of variant can change phenotype, but by different mechanisms. Learn this comparison, because exam questions often ask you to compare or to decide which kind of variant explains some data.
bullets: Non-coding variant: protein **normal**, **quantity** changed.
Coding variant: quantity **normal**, protein **structure and activity** changed.
Clue in data: if the protein is present but in a **lower concentration**, think non-coding variant.
Clue in data: if the protein is present in **normal amounts but does not work**, think coding variant.

head: Variant in non-coding DNA
Variant in coding DNA
rows: Due to more or less protein
Due to change in protein activity

callouts.p: Non-coding = how MUCH protein. Coding = what the protein is LIKE.

core.h: Worked context: sickle cell anaemia (coding variant)
core.p: A well known coding variant is in the gene for the beta chain of **haemoglobin**. A single **substitution** (A replaced by T) changes the triplet GAG to GTG, so the amino acid **glutamic acid** is replaced by **valine**. This changes how haemoglobin molecules behave: they stick together when oxygen is low, making red blood cells **sickle shaped**, which can block capillaries and carry less oxygen.
bullets: One base changed -> one amino acid changed -> haemoglobin shape and behaviour changed.
Amount of haemoglobin made is similar; its **properties** are different.
Shows how a tiny change in coding DNA can have a **large** effect on phenotype.
You do not need to memorise this example for Edexcel, but it is an excellent illustration in 6 mark answers.

callouts.p: Edexcel questions usually give you the context. Apply the chain of reasoning to whatever protein the question describes.

core.p: A person has **two copies** of each gene (one on each chromosome of a pair). Whether a variant shows in the phenotype can depend on the other copy. If one allele still makes enough working protein, the person may look normal; this is one reason many harmful variants are **recessive**.
bullets: Heterozygous person: one normal allele may make **enough functional protein**, so phenotype appears normal.
Homozygous for the variant: **no working protein**, so the phenotype is affected.
This links variants to inheritance of **recessive disorders** (for example cystic fibrosis).
Variants are inherited if they are in the DNA of **gametes**.

core.p: Examiners mark these questions by looking for each link in the chain. Missing a link (for example jumping from 'change in DNA' straight to 'protein does not work') loses marks. Write the chain step by step and use the key words.
bullets: Non-coding: **variant in non-coding DNA** / **RNA polymerase** binds less (or more) / **less (or more) transcription / mRNA** / **less (or more) protein** / phenotype changes.

Coding: **variant in coding DNA** / **change in triplet / codon** / **different amino acid sequence** / protein **folds differently** / **different shape** (for example active site) / **activity changes** / phenotype changes.
Use the words **quantity** for non-coding and **activity** for coding, as the spec does.
If asked to 'explain', always include **because** or **so** between each step.

callouts.p: Do not say the enzyme is 'killed' or 'dead'. Say its active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

analogy.p: Think of a gene as a recipe card in a factory. The non-coding region in front of it is the **'start' button** that the worker (RNA polymerase) presses. If the start button is sticky or damaged (a non-coding variant), the worker presses it less often, so **fewer cakes** are made, but each cake is perfect. The coding region is the **recipe itself**. A typo in the recipe (a coding variant), such as salt instead of sugar, means the **same number of cakes** is made but they **taste wrong** (the protein does not work properly). Where it breaks down: real RNA polymerase does not choose to press a button; binding depends on the shape of the protein fitting the DNA base sequence, and some recipe typos (silent substitutions) change nothing at all because several triplets code for the same amino acid.

terms.d: A difference in the DNA base sequence compared with the most common sequence.
A change in the base sequence of DNA; the cause of new genetic variants.
DNA whose base triplets code for the sequence of amino acids in a protein.
DNA that does not code for amino acids; some of it controls gene expression, for example where RNA polymerase binds.
The non-coding region of DNA in front of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription.
The enzyme that binds to non-coding DNA in front of a gene and joins RNA nucleotides to make mRNA during transcription.
Making an mRNA copy of a gene, using one DNA strand as a template, in the nucleus.
Using the codons on mRNA to join amino acids in the correct order at a ribosome.
A sequence of three DNA bases that codes for one amino acid.
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid.
The order of amino acids in a polypeptide, which determines how the protein folds and so its shape.
The part of an enzyme with a shape complementary to its substrate, where the substrate binds.
A mutation in which one base is replaced by a different base.
A change caused by inserting or deleting a base, so all following triplets are read differently.
Whether, and how much, a gene is transcribed and translated to make its protein.
The observable characteristics of an organism, produced by its genotype and environment.

mistakes.w: A variant in non-coding DNA changes the shape of the protein.
mistakes.r: Non-coding DNA does not code for amino acids, so the protein is unchanged; the variant changes RNA polymerase binding and so the amount of protein made.

mistakes.w: DNA polymerase binds to the non-coding region.
mistakes.r: RNA polymerase binds to the non-coding DNA in front of the gene to start transcription.

mistakes.w: Non-coding DNA is junk and has no effect.
mistakes.r: Non-coding DNA can control gene expression; variants in it can change how much protein is made and so change phenotype.

mistakes.w: A mutation always changes the protein.
mistakes.r: Many variants have no effect, for example a substitution that still codes for the same amino acid, or a variant outside important regions.

mistakes.w: The mutation changes the amino acid, so the enzyme is killed / denatured.
mistakes.r: The changed amino acid sequence makes the protein fold differently, changing the active site shape so the substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is not 'killed'.

mistakes.w: A coding variant means less protein is made.
mistakes.r: A coding variant changes the amino acid sequence and so the activity of the protein; the quantity is usually unchanged.

mistakes.w: Changes to the DNA change the base sequence of the amino acids.
mistakes.r: Changes to the DNA base sequence change the sequence of amino acids; amino acids do not have bases.

mistakes.w: Less RNA polymerase is made.
mistakes.r: The amount of RNA polymerase is the same; the variant changes how well it can bind to the DNA, so less mRNA is transcribed.

exam.q: State the name of the enzyme that binds to non-coding DNA in front of a gene.
model: RNA polymerase
exam.tip: Not DNA polymerase, and not 'polymerase' alone.

exam.q: State what is meant by a genetic variant.
model: A difference / change in the DNA base sequence (compared with the usual sequence)
exam.tip: Mention base sequence.

exam.q: A variant occurs in the non-coding DNA in front of a gene. Explain why the protein made from this gene still has a normal structure.
model: Non-coding DNA does not code for amino acids
So the coding DNA / triplets / amino acid sequence is unchanged
exam.tip: Link 'non-coding' to 'no change to amino acid sequence'.

exam.q: Describe how a genetic variant in the non-coding DNA of a gene can affect the phenotype of an organism.
model: Variant changes the binding of RNA polymerase (to the DNA / promoter)
Changes the amount of transcription / mRNA produced
So changes the quantity of protein produced
Changing the amount of the protein changes the characteristic / phenotype, e.g. less enzyme so less product
exam.tip: Four links in the chain: binding, transcription, quantity, phenotype.

exam.q: Describe how a genetic variant in the coding DNA of a gene can affect the phenotype of an organism.
model: Changes the base triplet / codon
Different amino acid (sequence) in the protein
Protein folds differently / has a different shape
Changes the activity of the protein, e.g. active site no longer fits substrate, so phenotype changes
exam.tip: Use the word activity for coding variants.

exam.q: A single base substitution in the coding DNA of a gene has no effect on the protein made. Suggest why.
model: The new triplet still codes for the same amino acid
(Because) more than one triplet can code for an amino acid / code is degenerate
exam.tip: Alternatively: the amino acid changed is not in an important part of the protein and does not affect its shape.

exam.q: Lactase is an enzyme that digests lactose. Some adults have a variant in the non-coding DNA near the lactase gene and produce lactase all their lives. Explain how this variant could allow these adults to digest milk.
model: Variant allows RNA polymerase to (continue to) bind to DNA
So the lactase gene is (still) transcribed / mRNA made
So lactase enzyme is produced and lactose can be broken down
exam.tip: Apply the non-coding chain to the context given.

exam.q: An enzyme in a plant makes a red pigment. In one plant, a variant in the coding DNA of this enzyme's gene changes one amino acid in the active site. Explain why this plant has white flowers.
model: Change in amino acid changes the shape of the active site
Substrate no longer fits / is not complementary / fewer enzyme-substrate complexes
So no (or less) red pigment made, flowers are white
exam.tip: Link the protein's changed activity to the phenotype in the question.

exam.q: Scientists measured the concentration of an enzyme in two groups of people. Group A had half the normal concentration of the enzyme; each enzyme molecule worked normally. Group B had normal concentration but the enzyme had very low activity. Suggest which group has a variant in non-coding DNA and which has a variant in coding DNA. Give reasons.
model: Group A: non-coding variant
Because quantity of protein changed but structure / activity normal (RNA polymerase binds less)
Group B: coding variant
Because amino acid sequence changed so shape / activity changed but amount the same
exam.tip: Quantity points to non-coding; activity points to coding.

exam.q: Explain how genetic variants in coding and non-coding DNA can each lead to a change in phenotype.
model: Non-coding DNA: variant can change binding of RNA polymerase
Changes rate of transcription / amount of mRNA
So changes quantity of protein made, e.g. less enzyme so less product
Coding DNA: variant changes base triplet so different amino acid (sequence)
Protein folds into different shape, e.g. active site changed so substrate does not fit
Changes activity of protein, so changes phenotype; some variants have no effect (e.g. same amino acid coded)
exam.tip: Structure a 6 marker in two clear halves, each with a full chain, then a final sentence on 'no effect'.

worked.q: A section of coding DNA reads CCT GAG GAG. A variant changes it to CCT GTG GAG. GAG codes for glutamic acid and GTG codes for valine. Explain the effect on the protein.
steps: Compare the sequences: the second triplet has changed from GAG to GTG, a substitution of A by T.
This changes the codon on mRNA, so a different amino acid is added during translation: valine instead of glutamic acid.
The amino acid sequence of the protein is now different at this position.
The protein may fold differently, changing its shape and properties (in haemoglobin this makes molecules stick together at low oxygen).
The amount of protein made is not changed, because the non-coding DNA where RNA polymerase binds is unchanged.
worked.ans: One amino acid is changed (glutamic acid to valine), which can change the protein's shape and activity, but not the quantity made.

worked.q: A plant gene makes an enzyme for purple pigment. Plant X has pale purple flowers. Its enzyme has a normal amino acid sequence but there is only 20% of the normal amount in its petal cells. Explain this phenotype.
steps: Normal amino acid sequence means the coding DNA is not affected, so the enzyme's shape and active site are normal.
Reduced amount means less of the protein is being made, so the problem is in gene expression.
So the variant is likely in the non-coding DNA where RNA polymerase binds.
RNA polymerase binds less easily, so less transcription and less mRNA, so less enzyme is translated.
Less enzyme means fewer enzyme-substrate complexes per second, so less purple pigment is made.
worked.ans: A non-coding variant reduces RNA polymerase binding, so less enzyme is made, less pigment forms and the flowers are pale.

worked.q: Model answer: Compare the effects of a variant in non-coding DNA and a variant in coding DNA on a protein.
steps: Both are changes in the base sequence of DNA that can change phenotype.
A non-coding variant affects the binding of RNA polymerase, so it changes how much mRNA, and so how much protein, is made.
A non-coding variant does not change the amino acid sequence, so any protein made has its normal shape and activity.
A coding variant changes a base triplet, so it can change the sequence of amino acids.
This can change how the protein folds and its shape, so its activity changes, although the quantity is usually the same.
worked.ans: Non-coding variants change the quantity of protein; coding variants change its amino acid sequence and so its activity.

bio_edx.2.6.summary: **Gregor Mendel**, a monk in Brno in the 1850s and 1860s, carried out careful breeding experiments on **pea plants** and counted thousands of offspring. From the ratios he saw (such as **3 tall : 1 dwarf** in the second generation) he proposed that characteristics are controlled by **separately inherited 'factors'** (now called genes and alleles) that do not blend, come in pairs and can be **dominant or recessive**. His work was largely ignored until **1900**, after his death, mainly because scientists at the time knew nothing about **chromosomes, genes or DNA**, his work was published in an obscure journal and his mathematical approach was unusual.

core.p: **Gregor Mendel** (1822 to 1884) was an Augustinian monk at a monastery in **Brno** (then Brünn, in the Austrian Empire, now in the Czech Republic). He had studied science and mathematics at the University of Vienna. Between about **1856 and 1863** he grew and bred thousands of **pea plants** in the monastery garden to find out how characteristics are passed from parents to offspring.
bullets: He was not a famous professional scientist, which later made it harder for his work to be noticed.
His training in **maths and statistics** led him to **count** offspring and look for **ratios**, which was unusual in biology at the time.
He presented his results in **1865** and published them in **1866** in the journal of the Natural History Society of Brno.
He became abbot of the monastery and did much less research in later life; he died in **1884**.

callouts.p: Experiments about 1856 to 1863; published 1866; died 1884; work rediscovered in 1900.

core.h: The big question before Mendel: blending inheritance
core.p: In the mid 1800s most scientists believed in **blending inheritance**: that characteristics of the two parents mix together in the offspring, like mixing paints. This predicts that a tall plant crossed with a dwarf plant would give medium plants, and that a characteristic, once blended, could never reappear in its original form. Mendel's results showed this was wrong.
bullets: Blending predicts **intermediate** offspring every time.
Blending predicts that a characteristic that disappears can **never come back**.
Mendel found that a characteristic could **disappear in one generation and reappear unchanged** in the next.
This showed that the 'factor' for the characteristic must have been **passed on intact**, not blended.

callouts.p: The old (incorrect) idea that the characteristics of both parents mix together to give an intermediate offspring.

core.p: Mendel's choice of organism was a big part of his success. Pea plants have features that make breeding experiments quick, controlled and easy to count.
bullets: Peas have characteristics with **two clear, contrasting forms** (for example tall or dwarf), with no in-between forms, so offspring are easy to classify.
They **grow quickly** and produce **many seeds**, so large numbers of offspring can be counted, making results reliable.
Peas normally **self-pollinate**, so Mendel could breed **true-breeding** lines (plants that always produce offspring like themselves).
Mendel could also control **cross-pollination** by removing the anthers of one flower and transferring pollen from another plant with a brush.
He studied **seven characteristics**, including stem height, seed shape (round or wrinkled), seed colour (yellow or green) and flower colour (purple or white).

callouts.p: Do not just say 'peas were easy to grow'. Say why it helped: large numbers of offspring so ratios are reliable; clear contrasting forms so offspring are easy to classify.

core.p: Mendel's method was careful and **controlled**, and he repeated it for each characteristic. He started with **true-breeding** parents that differed in only one characteristic, crossed them, then let the offspring **self-pollinate** and counted the next generation.
bullets: Step 1: Bred **true-breeding** tall plants and true-breeding dwarf plants for several generations to be sure they were pure.
Step 2: **Cross-pollinated** a tall plant with a dwarf plant (the parental, or P, generation), preventing self-pollination by removing anthers.
Step 3: Grew the seeds and recorded the **first generation (F1)** offspring.
Step 4: Allowed the F1 plants to **self-pollinate**, grew the seeds and **counted** the **second generation (F2)**.
Step 5: Calculated **ratios** and repeated with each of the seven characteristics, using very large numbers of plants.

callouts.p: Large sample sizes, one characteristic at a time, true-breeding parents and controlled pollination made Mendel's results valid and repeatable.

core.p: When he crossed true-breeding tall plants with true-breeding dwarf plants, **all the F1 plants were tall**; none were medium height. When the F1 plants self-pollinated, the **dwarf form reappeared** in the F2, in about **one quarter** of the plants. In one experiment he counted **787 tall and 277 dwarf** plants, a ratio of about **2.84 : 1**, which is close to **3 : 1**. He saw similar 3 : 1 ratios for the other characteristics, for example 5474 round seeds to 1850 wrinkled seeds.
bullets: F1: **100% tall**, so the tall form **masks** the dwarf form.
F2: about **3 tall : 1 dwarf**, so the dwarf factor was still there, hidden, in the F1.
No **intermediate** plants at any stage, so factors do not blend.
The same pattern for all seven characteristics suggested a **general rule** of inheritance.

callouts.p: 787 / 277 = 2.84, so the ratio is 2.84 : 1, which is approximately 3 : 1.

fig.cap: Mendel's monohybrid cross for stem height. True-breeding tall and dwarf parents gave all-tall F1 plants. Self-pollinating the F1 gave an F2 of 787 tall and 277 dwarf, about 3 : 1, so the dwarf characteristic reappeared unchanged.

core.p: To explain his ratios, Mendel proposed that each characteristic is controlled by **inherited 'factors'** (we now call them **genes**, and the different versions **alleles**). His key ideas were that factors are passed on **separately and unchanged**, so they do not blend, and that the offspring receive factors from **both parents**.
bullets: Each characteristic is controlled by **inherited factors** that are passed from parents to offspring.
Each individual has **two factors** for each characteristic, one inherited **from each parent**.
When gametes form, the two factors **separate**, so each gamete carries **only one** factor.
Some factors are **dominant** and mask others, which are **recessive**; a recessive characteristic only shows if **both** factors are recessive.
Factors are passed on **unchanged**, which is why the dwarf form could reappear in the F2.

callouts.p: Mendel proposed separately inherited factors because a characteristic hidden in the F1 reappeared unchanged in the F2, so the factor must have been passed on as a separate unit, not blended.

core.h: Explaining the 3 : 1 ratio with modern genetics
core.p: Using alleles, the results make sense. True-breeding tall plants are **TT** and true-breeding dwarf plants are **tt**. All F1 plants receive one T and one t, so they are **Tt** and tall. When two Tt plants are crossed, each produces gametes T and t in equal numbers, giving offspring **TT, Tt, Tt and tt** in a **1 : 2 : 1** genotype ratio and a **3 tall : 1 dwarf** phenotype ratio.
bullets: P: TT x tt; gametes T and t.
F1: all **Tt** (heterozygous), all tall because T is dominant.
F1 cross: Tt x Tt; gametes T or t from each parent.
F2 genotypes: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt; phenotypes: **3 tall : 1 dwarf**.
Mendel did not know about alleles; he worked this pattern out from the numbers alone.

callouts.p: A 3 : 1 ratio means a probability of 0.75 (75%) tall and 0.25 (25%) dwarf for each offspring of a Tt x Tt cross.

fig.cap: Punnett square for crossing two F1 plants (Tt x Tt). Each parent makes T and t gametes, giving TT, Tt, Tt and tt: three tall to one dwarf, matching Mendel's F2 ratio.

core.h: Why Mendel's work was not recognised in his lifetime
core.p: Mendel's work is now seen as the foundation of genetics, but almost nobody took notice of it while he was alive. Edexcel expects you to explain several reasons, and the most important is that there was **no known mechanism**: scientists had not yet discovered chromosomes, genes or DNA, so his invisible 'factors' seemed to have no physical basis.
bullets: **No mechanism**: scientists did not know about **genes, chromosomes or DNA**, so they could not see how 'factors' could exist or be passed on.
**Obscure publication**: published in the journal of a small local natural history society, so few leading scientists read it.
**Unknown scientist**: Mendel was a monk, not a well known university scientist, so his work carried little authority.
**Unusual maths**: using **statistics and ratios** in biology was new, and many biologists did not understand or value it.
**Against accepted ideas**: most scientists believed in **blending inheritance**, so a theory of separate, unchanging factors seemed strange.
**Did not seem to apply widely**: when Mendel repeated his work on another plant (hawkweed), the results did not follow the same pattern, so the rules seemed limited.
He became abbot and largely **stopped his research**, so he did not promote his ideas.

callouts.p: His work was not recognised because scientists at the time did not know about genes, chromosomes or DNA, so there was no explanation of how his factors worked.
Mendel's conclusions were correct. They were ignored for reasons of communication and lack of a mechanism, not because his data were poor.

core.p: In **1900**, 16 years after Mendel's death, botanists including **Hugo de Vries** and **Carl Correns** independently carried out similar experiments, found the same ratios and then found Mendel's paper. Around the same time, improved microscopes showed **chromosomes** and how they behave when cells divide. Scientists realised that chromosomes come in **pairs** and **separate** when gametes form, exactly as Mendel's factors did, so Mendel's factors must be carried on chromosomes.
bullets: Late 1800s: chromosomes observed in dividing cells.
1900: Mendel's work **rediscovered** and confirmed by other scientists.
Early 1900s: behaviour of chromosomes in **meiosis** matched the behaviour of Mendel's factors; the word **gene** came into use.
1953: **Watson and Crick** worked out the double helix structure of **DNA**, explaining what genes are made of.
Later work showed that genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins, completing the mechanism Mendel lacked.

callouts.p: Mendel's story shows that new ideas are often accepted only when other scientists can repeat the results and when an explanation (mechanism) is found.

fig.cap: Timeline of Mendel's work: experiments in 1856 to 1863, publication in 1866, his death in 1884, rediscovery in 1900 by de Vries and Correns, and the discovery of DNA structure in 1953 which explained what his factors are.

core.p: Mendel's ideas are the basis of all **monohybrid inheritance** that you study at GCSE: genetic diagrams, Punnett squares, dominant and recessive alleles, and predicting ratios and probabilities. His work also explained how variation can be **kept** in a population, which helped support Darwin's theory of **natural selection**.
bullets: Showed inheritance follows **predictable rules** that can be described with ratios.
Introduced the idea of **dominant** and **recessive** characteristics.
Showed that hidden (recessive) characteristics can be **carried** and reappear in later generations.
Blending would gradually remove variation; Mendel's factors **preserve variation**, which natural selection needs.
Founded the science of **genetics**.

core.p: Exam questions may ask you to evaluate Mendel's method. Think about what made it valid and repeatable, and what he could not know.
bullets: Strength: **very large sample sizes** reduce the effect of chance, so ratios are reliable.
Strength: **true-breeding** parents and **controlled pollination** meant he knew exactly which plants were crossed.
Strength: studied **one characteristic at a time**, with clear contrasting forms.
Strength: results were **repeatable** for seven different characteristics.

Limitation: characteristics he chose happened to be controlled by **single genes** with complete dominance; many characteristics are controlled by **many genes** and the environment, so do not give simple ratios.
Limitation: he could not explain the **mechanism**, because chromosomes and DNA were unknown.

callouts.p: Fertilisation is random, so observed ratios are close to but not exactly 3 : 1. Larger samples give ratios closer to the expected value.

analogy.t: Marbles in a bag, not paint in a pot
analogy.p: Blending inheritance treats characteristics like **paint**: mix red and white and you get pink forever, and you can never get pure red back. Mendel showed inheritance is more like **marbles**: each parent puts one marble (factor) into each offspring. A tall marble and a dwarf marble together look tall because the tall marble is dominant, but the dwarf marble is still there, unchanged, and can be passed on, so two hidden dwarf marbles can come together later and a dwarf plant reappears. Where it breaks down: real factors are sections of DNA on chromosomes, not separate objects, and many characteristics are controlled by several genes and by the environment, so they do not behave as simply as single marbles.

terms.d: A monk in Brno (1822 to 1884) whose breeding experiments with pea plants led to the idea of separately inherited factors.
Mendel's name for the unit that controls a characteristic and is passed from parent to offspring; now called a gene.
The incorrect idea that characteristics of the two parents mix to give intermediate offspring.
A plant that always produces offspring with the same characteristic as itself when self-pollinated (homozygous).
Transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or plant.
Transfer of pollen from one plant to the stigma of a different plant.
The parental generation in a breeding experiment.
The first generation of offspring from a cross between the parents.
The second generation, produced by crossing or self-pollinating F1 individuals.
A characteristic (allele) that is expressed even if only one copy is present.
A characteristic (allele) that is only expressed if two copies are present; hidden when a dominant allele is present.
The relative number of offspring with each phenotype, for example 3 : 1.
A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein; the modern name for Mendel's factor.
A different version of the same gene; Mendel's alternative forms of a factor.
A long, coiled molecule of DNA carrying many genes; found in pairs in body cells.
A cross that follows the inheritance of a single characteristic controlled by one gene.

mistakes.w: Mendel discovered genes and DNA.
mistakes.r: Mendel proposed 'inherited factors'; he knew nothing about genes, chromosomes or DNA, which were discovered or understood later.

mistakes.w: His work was ignored because his results were wrong.
mistakes.r: His results were correct; they were ignored because scientists did not know about chromosomes/genes/DNA (no mechanism), and his paper was in an obscure journal.

mistakes.w: Mendel worked with fruit flies.
mistakes.r: Mendel worked with pea plants.

mistakes.w: The F1 plants were medium height.
mistakes.r: All F1 plants were tall; there were no intermediate plants, showing factors do not blend.

mistakes.w: The dwarf factor was lost in the F1 generation.
mistakes.r: The dwarf factor was still present but hidden (recessive) in the F1, which is why dwarf plants reappeared in the F2.

mistakes.w: Mendel's work was recognised during his lifetime.
mistakes.r: It was largely ignored until 1900, after his death in 1884, when it was rediscovered.

mistakes.w: The F2 ratio was 1 : 2 : 1 tall to dwarf.
mistakes.r: The phenotype ratio was 3 tall : 1 dwarf; 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotype ratio (TT : Tt : tt).

mistakes.w: Mendel used a few plants.
mistakes.r: He used very large numbers of plants, which made his ratios reliable.

exam.q: Name the organism Gregor Mendel used in his breeding experiments.
model: Pea plant
exam.tip: One word answer, 'peas' is fine.

exam.q: Give one reason why Mendel's work was not recognised during his lifetime.
model: Scientists did not know about genes / chromosomes / DNA (so no mechanism) OR published in an obscure journal OR he was not a well known scientist OR use of maths was unusual
exam.tip: The 'no knowledge of genes/chromosomes/DNA' reason is the safest.

exam.q: Mendel crossed true-breeding tall pea plants with true-breeding dwarf pea plants. State what he observed in the F1 generation.
model: All the offspring were tall
exam.tip: Say 'all tall', not 'mostly tall'.

exam.q: In the F2 generation Mendel counted 787 tall and 277 dwarf plants. Calculate the ratio of tall to dwarf plants.
model: Ratio = 2.84 : 1 (approximately 3 : 1)
exam.tip: Divide the larger by the smaller to get x : 1.

exam.q: Explain why Mendel's results did not support the idea of blending inheritance.
model: The F1 were all tall, not intermediate / medium height
The dwarf characteristic reappeared (unchanged) in the F2, which would not happen if characteristics blended
exam.tip: Use both generations as evidence.

exam.q: Give two reasons why pea plants were a good choice for Mendel's experiments.
model: Characteristics have two clear contrasting forms / easy to classify
Grow quickly / produce many offspring so large samples
Can control pollination / can self-pollinate to give true-breeding lines
exam.tip: Any two; explain the benefit briefly.

exam.q: Describe what Mendel concluded about inheritance from his experiments.
model: Characteristics are controlled by inherited factors that are passed on separately / unchanged
Each organism has two factors for each characteristic, one from each parent
Some factors are dominant and others recessive / dominant masks recessive
exam.tip: Use Mendel's word 'factors' and link to dominant and recessive.

exam.q: Explain why Mendel proposed the idea of separately inherited factors.
model: Crossing tall and dwarf gave all tall offspring / no intermediates
The dwarf characteristic reappeared in the F2 generation (in about a quarter)
So the factor for dwarf must have been passed on unchanged / separately and not blended
exam.tip: Data first, then the conclusion.

exam.q: Explain why the importance of Mendel's work was not recognised until after his death.
model: Scientists had not discovered genes / chromosomes / DNA
So there was no mechanism to explain his factors
Work was published in an obscure / little-read journal; Mendel not a well known scientist
Use of mathematics / statistics in biology was unusual; most scientists believed in blending inheritance
Work was rediscovered in 1900 when chromosomes were understood
exam.tip: Any four points; lead with the mechanism reason.

exam.q: Describe Mendel's experiments on pea plants and explain how his findings, and later discoveries, led to our modern understanding of inheritance.
model: Used true-breeding tall and dwarf plants and cross-pollinated them
F1 all tall; F1 self-pollinated and large numbers of F2 counted
F2 about 3 tall : 1 dwarf, no intermediates
Concluded characteristics controlled by separately inherited factors, in pairs, dominant and recessive
Not accepted at the time because genes / chromosomes / DNA unknown; obscure journal
Rediscovered in 1900; chromosomes / genes shown to behave like his factors; DNA structure 1953 explained what factors are
exam.tip: Organise as method, results, conclusion, recognition, later evidence.

worked.q: In another experiment Mendel counted 5474 round seeds and 1850 wrinkled seeds in the F2. Calculate the ratio and the percentage of wrinkled seeds, and explain what they show.
steps: Ratio: 5474 / 1850 = 2.96, so 2.96 : 1, approximately 3 : 1.
Percentage wrinkled = 1850 / 7324 x 100 = 25.3%.
This is close to the 25% expected for a recessive characteristic from a cross between two heterozygous parents.
It shows round is dominant and the wrinkled factor was hidden in the F1 but passed on unchanged.
worked.ans: Ratio about 2.96 : 1 (3 : 1); 25.3% wrinkled, showing round is dominant and wrinkled is recessive.

worked.q: Use modern genetic symbols to explain Mendel's results for tall and dwarf plants. Use T for tall and t for dwarf.
steps: True-breeding tall = TT; true-breeding dwarf = tt.
Gametes: TT parent makes only T; tt parent makes only t.
F1 = all Tt; T is dominant so all are tall.
F1 x F1: Tt x Tt; each parent makes T and t gametes in equal numbers.
F2 genotypes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt = 1 : 2 : 1; phenotypes 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
worked.ans: F1 all Tt (tall); F2 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, giving 3 tall : 1 dwarf, matching Mendel's data.

worked.q: Model answer: Suggest why Mendel's ideas were accepted after 1900 but not in 1866.
steps: In 1866 nobody knew about chromosomes, genes or DNA, so his factors had no known physical form or mechanism.
His paper was in a small local journal and he was an unknown monk, so few scientists read it.
By 1900 other scientists had repeated similar experiments and got the same results, confirming his work.
Chromosomes had been seen, and their behaviour in gamete formation matched Mendel's factors (in pairs, separating).
This provided a mechanism, so the scientific community accepted the theory.
worked.ans: By 1900 his results had been repeated and chromosomes provided a mechanism for his factors, which was missing in 1866.

bio_edx.2.7.summary: Genes are sections of DNA on **chromosomes**, and most genes come in different versions called **alleles**. Because body cells have **pairs** of chromosomes, each person has **two alleles** of every gene, one from each parent, carried into the **zygote** by the **gametes**. Differences in inherited characteristics arise because different alleles code for slightly different proteins and because individuals inherit different **combinations** of alleles. You must be able to define and use **chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, gamete and zygote** precisely.

core.p: The nucleus of a human body cell contains **46 chromosomes** arranged in **23 pairs**. Each chromosome is one very long, coiled molecule of **DNA**, and along it are many **genes**. A gene is a short section of DNA that **codes for a specific protein**, and that protein helps to produce a characteristic.
bullets: Chromosomes are found in the **nucleus**.
Chromosomes come in **pairs**: one of each pair came from the **mother** and one from the **father**.
The two chromosomes of a pair carry the **same genes** in the **same positions**.
Each gene codes for a **sequence of amino acids**, making a specific **protein** (for example an enzyme or a pigment).

callouts.p: A long, coiled molecule of DNA, found in the nucleus, that carries many genes.
A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein.

core.h: Alleles: different versions of a gene
core.p: Most genes exist in **two or more different forms**, called **alleles**. Alleles of a gene have slightly different **base sequences**, so they can code for slightly different versions of the protein. For example, a pea plant gene for flower colour has an allele for **purple** and an allele for **white**. Because chromosomes are in pairs, every individual has **two alleles** of each gene, which may be the **same** or **different**.
bullets: An allele is a **version** of a gene, not a different gene.
Different alleles have **different base sequences**.
Different base sequences can give a **different amino acid sequence**, so a different protein (or no working protein).
Alleles are found at the **same position** on each chromosome of a pair.
An individual has **two** alleles of each gene; a population can contain **many** alleles of the same gene.

callouts.p: A different version (form) of the same gene.

fig.cap: Three possible pairs of alleles for the pea flower colour gene. The gene is at the same position on both chromosomes of a pair. PP and pp are homozygous (same alleles); Pp is heterozygous (different alleles). Because purple (P) is dominant, PP and Pp plants both have purple flowers; only pp plants are white.

core.h: From nucleus to allele: the hierarchy
core.p: Students often muddle these words, so learn them as a size order. The **nucleus** contains **chromosomes**; each chromosome is made of **DNA** and carries many **genes**; each gene can exist as different **alleles**.
bullets: Nucleus > chromosome > gene > allele (from largest to most specific).
The **genome** is the entire genetic material of an organism.
A gene is a **position and a job**; an allele is the **particular version** at that position.
Saying 'the gene for blue eyes' is loose: strictly it is an **allele** that gives blue eyes.

callouts.p: If a question asks about different versions of a characteristic, the answer is almost always 'alleles', not 'genes'.

core.p: When an individual has two different alleles, often only one of them affects the phenotype. The allele that is **always expressed, even if only one copy is present**, is **dominant**. The allele that is **only expressed when two copies are present** (no dominant allele) is **recessive**. Dominant alleles are written with a **capital letter** and recessive alleles with the **same letter in lower case**.
bullets: Dominant allele: shows in the phenotype in **PP** and **Pp** individuals.
Recessive allele: shows in the phenotype **only in pp** individuals.
In a heterozygote the recessive allele is still **present and can be passed on** to offspring, even though it is hidden.
Often the dominant allele codes for a **working protein** and the recessive allele for a **non-working** one; one working copy can make **enough protein**, so the dominant characteristic shows.
Dominant does **not** mean more common or better; it only describes which allele is expressed.

callouts.p: An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present (no dominant allele is present).
Use one letter whose capital and lower case look different, e.g. B and b, not S and s or C and c. Never use two different letters for alleles of one gene.

core.p: These words describe whether the **two alleles** of a gene in one individual are the **same or different**. **Homo-** means same and **hetero-** means different.
bullets: **Homozygous**: both alleles the **same**, e.g. PP (homozygous dominant) or pp (homozygous recessive).
**Heterozygous**: the two alleles are **different**, e.g. Pp.
Homozygous individuals produce gametes that **all carry the same allele**; heterozygous individuals produce **two types** of gamete in equal numbers.
A **true-breeding** organism is homozygous for that gene.
A heterozygous individual for a recessive disorder is called a **carrier**: it has the allele but not the disorder.

callouts.p: Having two identical alleles of a particular gene.
Having two different alleles of a particular gene.

core.p: The **genotype** is the **combination of alleles** an individual has for a gene, written with letters (for example Pp). The **phenotype** is the **observable characteristic** that results, such as purple flowers. Phenotype depends on the genotype and, for many characteristics, also on the **environment**.
bullets: Genotype = **letters** (alleles); phenotype = **words** describing what you see or measure.
Two different genotypes (PP and Pp) can give the **same phenotype** because of dominance.
You can always work out the genotype of an individual showing the **recessive** phenotype: it must be homozygous recessive.
You **cannot** tell from the phenotype alone whether a dominant-phenotype individual is homozygous or heterozygous.
Environment can alter phenotype, e.g. a plant with alleles for tallness will be short if grown in poor light or soil.

callouts.p: The combination of alleles an individual has for a particular gene.
The observable characteristics of an individual, resulting from its genotype (and the environment).
'Pp' is a genotype; 'purple flowers' is a phenotype. Writing 'the phenotype is Pp' loses the mark.

core.p: **Gametes** are the sex cells: **sperm and egg cells** in animals, **pollen nuclei and egg cells** in flowering plants. They are made by **meiosis** and are **haploid**, containing **one set of chromosomes** (23 in humans) and so only **one allele of each gene**. At **fertilisation**, a male and a female gamete fuse to form a **zygote**, which is **diploid** (46 chromosomes in humans), with **two alleles of each gene**, one from each parent.
bullets: Gametes are haploid so that the chromosome number is **restored**, not doubled, at fertilisation.
Each gamete gets **one chromosome from each pair**, so it carries only **one allele** of each gene.
Which allele a gamete gets is **random**, which is why siblings inherit different combinations.
The zygote divides by **mitosis** to form the embryo; every body cell has the same genotype as the zygote.

callouts.p: A sex cell (sperm or egg in animals) containing half the normal number of chromosomes (haploid).
The diploid cell formed when the nuclei of a male gamete and a female gamete fuse at fertilisation.

fig.cap: Body cells are diploid (46 chromosomes in humans). Meiosis makes haploid gametes (23 chromosomes, one allele of each gene). At fertilisation a sperm and egg fuse to form a diploid zygote, which has two alleles of each gene, one from each parent.

core.h: Why alleles cause differences in inherited characteristics
core.p: This is what spec point 3.12 asks you to explain. Individuals of the same species have the **same genes**, but they can have **different alleles** of those genes. Different alleles have different base sequences, so they can code for **different versions of a protein** (or for no working protein), which gives a **different characteristic**. In addition, each individual inherits a **different combination** of alleles from its parents.
bullets: Different alleles -> different **base sequence** -> different **amino acid sequence** -> different **protein** -> different **characteristic**.
Each person inherits **one allele of each gene from each parent**, so their genotype is a **new combination**.
Meiosis puts alleles into gametes **randomly**, and **fertilisation is random**, so even siblings differ (except identical twins).
Whether an allele shows depends on **dominance**: a recessive allele can be hidden for generations, then appear when two copies come together.
With thousands of genes, each with possible different alleles, the number of possible combinations is enormous, which is why individuals vary so much.

callouts.p: Same genes, different alleles; alleles code for different proteins; offspring inherit different combinations of alleles from their parents; dominant alleles mask recessive alleles; so inherited characteristics differ.

core.p: Exam questions often describe a situation and ask you to use the terms correctly. Practise turning a description into the precise vocabulary.
bullets: 'A pea plant has one purple allele and one white allele' -> genotype **Pp**, **heterozygous**, phenotype **purple**.
'A plant has white flowers' -> genotype **pp**, **homozygous recessive**.
'A plant has purple flowers' -> genotype **PP or Pp**; you cannot tell which from phenotype alone.
'Pollen from a Pp plant' -> each pollen nucleus (gamete) carries **either P or p**, never both.
'A Pp plant fertilises a pp plant' -> zygotes are Pp or pp, each with **two alleles**.

callouts.p: Always circle single letters for gametes (P, p). A gamete written as 'Pp' is wrong because gametes are haploid.

core.p: An **individual** can only have **two** alleles of a gene (one on each chromosome of the pair), but a **population** can have **more than two** different alleles of the same gene. For example, the human ABO blood group gene has three alleles in the population, but each person has only two of them.
bullets: Individual (diploid body cell): **two** alleles per gene.
Gamete (haploid): **one** allele per gene.
Population: can contain **many** alleles of a gene.
Most characteristics (such as height) are controlled by **several genes** acting together, not just one, and are also affected by the environment.

callouts.p: Single-gene examples are used to learn the terms, but most human characteristics are controlled by many genes.

core.h: Quick definitions to learn word for word
core.p: These are the definitions Edexcel mark schemes accept. Learn them exactly.
bullets: **Chromosome**: a long coiled DNA molecule carrying many genes.
**Gene**: a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.
**Allele**: a different version of a gene.
**Dominant**: always expressed, even if only one copy present.
**Recessive**: only expressed if two copies present.
**Homozygous**: two identical alleles. **Heterozygous**: two different alleles.
**Genotype**: the alleles an individual has. **Phenotype**: the characteristics shown.
**Gamete**: haploid sex cell. **Zygote**: diploid cell formed when gametes fuse at fertilisation.

head: Term
Example (pea flower colour)
rows: Pollen nucleus or egg cell carrying P or p

analogy.p: Think of your chromosomes as **pairs of recipe books**, one book of each pair from your mother and one from your father. Each book has the same recipes (genes) on the same pages, such as 'flower colour'. But the two books may have **different versions** of a recipe (alleles): one says 'make purple pigment', the other has a misprint so no pigment is made. If either book has the working recipe, the cell can follow it and you see purple (dominant). You only see white if **both** books have the misprint (recessive). When you make gametes, you pass on **one book from each pair**, chosen at random. Where it breaks down: cells do not 'choose' a recipe; both alleles can be read, and dominance is usually because one working allele makes enough protein, and in some genes both alleles show (codominance).

terms.d: A long, coiled molecule of DNA, found in the nucleus, that carries many genes.
A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein.
A different version (form) of the same gene.
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present.
Having two identical alleles of a particular gene.
Having two different alleles of a particular gene.
The combination of alleles an individual has for a particular gene.
The observable characteristics of an individual, resulting from its genotype and the environment.
A haploid sex cell (sperm or egg in animals; pollen nucleus or egg in plants).
The diploid cell formed when the nuclei of a male and a female gamete fuse at fertilisation.
Having one set of chromosomes (23 in humans), as in gametes.
Having two sets of chromosomes, in pairs (46 in humans), as in body cells.
The fusion of a male gamete nucleus with a female gamete nucleus.
A heterozygous individual who has one recessive allele for a disorder but does not have the disorder.
The entire genetic material of an organism.

mistakes.w: An allele is a gene.
mistakes.r: An allele is a different version of a gene; a gene can have two or more alleles.

mistakes.w: The phenotype is Bb.
mistakes.r: Bb is the genotype (the alleles); the phenotype is the characteristic shown, e.g. brown fur.

mistakes.w: A dominant allele is the one that is most common.
mistakes.r: A dominant allele is one that is expressed even if only one copy is present; it is not necessarily the most common.

mistakes.w: Heterozygous means having two of the same alleles.
mistakes.r: Heterozygous means having two different alleles; homozygous means two identical alleles.

mistakes.w: A gamete contains two alleles of each gene.
mistakes.r: A gamete is haploid and contains only one allele of each gene.

mistakes.w: A recessive allele is not passed on in a heterozygote.
mistakes.r: The recessive allele is still present and can be passed on in gametes, even though it is not expressed.

mistakes.w: Using different letters for the alleles, e.g. B for brown and w for white.
mistakes.r: Use the same letter: a capital for the dominant allele and lower case for the recessive allele (B and b).

mistakes.w: A zygote is haploid.
mistakes.r: A zygote is diploid because it contains a set of chromosomes from each gamete.

mistakes.w: A gene is a chromosome.
mistakes.r: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule that carries many genes; a gene is one section of it.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term allele.
model: A different form / version of a gene
exam.tip: Do not just write 'a gene'.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term heterozygous.
model: Having two different alleles (of a gene)
exam.tip: Hetero = different.

exam.q: Name the cell formed when two gametes fuse at fertilisation.
model: Zygote
exam.tip: Not embryo; the zygote comes first.

exam.q: In cats, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant to the allele for brown fur (b). Give the genotype of a brown cat and state whether it is homozygous or heterozygous.
model: bb
Homozygous (recessive)
exam.tip: A recessive phenotype always means homozygous recessive.

exam.q: Explain the difference between genotype and phenotype.
model: Genotype is the alleles / combination of alleles an organism has
Phenotype is the observable characteristic(s) of the organism
exam.tip: Give one clear definition for each word.

exam.q: Explain why a cat with black fur could have the genotype BB or Bb.
model: B is dominant / is expressed if only one copy is present
So one B allele is enough to give black fur / b is masked by B
exam.tip: Link dominant to 'one copy is enough'.

exam.q: Explain why a human gamete contains 23 chromosomes but a zygote contains 46.
model: Gametes are made by meiosis and are haploid / contain one chromosome from each pair
At fertilisation two gametes fuse (23 + 23)
So the zygote is diploid / has 23 pairs, with one chromosome of each pair from each parent
exam.tip: Mention that halving prevents doubling each generation.

exam.q: A pea plant has the genotype Tt. State the alleles that can be found in its gametes and explain why.
model: Either T or t (half of gametes each)
Because gametes are haploid / contain only one chromosome of each pair, so only one allele of each gene
exam.tip: A gamete is never Tt.

exam.q: Explain why there are differences in the inherited characteristics of individuals of the same species.
model: Individuals have the same genes but can have different alleles
Different alleles have different base sequences / code for different proteins
Offspring inherit one allele of each gene from each parent / a different combination of alleles
Random assortment in meiosis and random fertilisation give each individual a unique combination; dominant alleles can mask recessive ones
exam.tip: Mention both 'different alleles' and 'different combinations'.

exam.q: Using the terms chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous and heterozygous, explain how two purple-flowered pea plants can produce a white-flowered offspring.
model: Flower colour is controlled by a gene on a chromosome; the gene has two alleles, purple (P) and white (p)
P is dominant, p is recessive, so a plant with at least one P is purple
Both parents must be heterozygous (Pp), so each carries a hidden recessive p allele
Each gamete contains only one allele, P or p, because gametes are haploid
If two gametes carrying p fuse at fertilisation, the zygote is pp
A pp plant is homozygous recessive, so the recessive allele is expressed and flowers are white
exam.tip: Use every listed term at least once, correctly.

worked.q: A mouse with grey fur has genotype Gg; a mouse with white fur has genotype gg. Identify the dominant allele, describe each mouse's genotype, and give the alleles in each mouse's gametes.
steps: The heterozygous mouse (Gg) is grey, so the grey allele G must be dominant and white (g) recessive.
Gg mouse: heterozygous; phenotype grey.
gg mouse: homozygous recessive; phenotype white.
Gg mouse's gametes: half carry G and half carry g (one allele per haploid gamete).
gg mouse's gametes: all carry g.
worked.ans: G (grey) is dominant. Gg is heterozygous and makes G or g gametes; gg is homozygous recessive and makes only g gametes.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why a heterozygous individual shows the dominant characteristic.
steps: A heterozygous individual has two different alleles of the gene, e.g. Pp.
The dominant allele (P) codes for a working protein, e.g. an enzyme that makes purple pigment.
One copy of the dominant allele produces enough of the protein for the characteristic to show.
The recessive allele (p) may code for a non-working protein, so it has no visible effect when P is present.
So the dominant allele is expressed and the recessive allele is masked, but it can still be passed on.
worked.ans: The single dominant allele makes enough functional protein for the characteristic to appear, masking the recessive allele.

worked.q: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes and alleles per gene in (a) a sperm cell, (b) a zygote, and explain.
steps: Sperm is a gamete made by meiosis, so it is haploid: 23 chromosomes.
It has one chromosome from each pair, so one allele of each gene.
At fertilisation sperm (23) fuses with egg (23): 23 + 23 = 46.
The zygote is diploid: 23 pairs of chromosomes.
It has two alleles of each gene, one from the father and one from the mother.
worked.ans: (a) Sperm: 23 chromosomes, one allele per gene. (b) Zygote: 46 chromosomes, two alleles per gene.

bio_edx.2.8.summary: Monohybrid inheritance is the inheritance of a characteristic controlled by **one gene** with two alleles, one dominant and one recessive. Because each parent passes on only one allele in each gamete, we can predict the possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring using a **genetic diagram** or a **Punnett square**, and we can work backwards from a **family pedigree** to deduce who carries a recessive allele. Grade 9 answers set out every stage clearly (parents, gametes, offspring, ratio) and explain each deduction using the words dominant, recessive, homozygous and heterozygous.

core.p: A **monohybrid cross** follows the inheritance of just **one characteristic** controlled by **a single gene**. The gene has two versions, called **alleles**. Every body cell has two copies of each chromosome (one from each parent), so it has two alleles of the gene. Gametes are made by meiosis, so each gamete carries only **one** allele.
bullets: Mono = one gene being followed; hybrid = offspring of a cross.
Body cells are **diploid**: two alleles of each gene.
Gametes are **haploid**: one allele of each gene.
At fertilisation, one allele from the egg and one from the sperm combine, restoring two alleles.
Which allele goes into a particular gamete is a matter of **chance**, so we can only predict **probabilities**, not exact outcomes.

callouts.p: The inheritance of a single characteristic controlled by one gene with different alleles.

core.p: A **dominant** allele is expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present. A **recessive** allele is only expressed when **two copies** are present, because otherwise the dominant allele masks it. We use a **capital letter** for the dominant allele and the **same letter in lower case** for the recessive allele.
bullets: Choose a letter whose capital and lower case look different, such as B and b, not C and c, S and s or O and o.
BB = **homozygous dominant**: shows the dominant phenotype.
Bb = **heterozygous**: shows the dominant phenotype but carries the recessive allele.
bb = **homozygous recessive**: the only genotype that shows the recessive phenotype.
A person who is heterozygous for a recessive disorder is called a **carrier**.

head: Genotype
Name
Phenotype (B = black fur, b = white fur)

callouts.p: A dominant allele is not necessarily the most common allele in a population and is not 'stronger' or better. It simply masks the recessive allele in a heterozygote.

core.p: The **genotype** is the combination of alleles an organism has (for example Bb). The **phenotype** is the observable characteristic that results (for example black fur). Two organisms can have the same phenotype but different genotypes, which is why we cannot always tell genotype by looking.
bullets: BB and Bb both give the dominant phenotype.
The recessive phenotype always tells you the genotype: it must be homozygous recessive.
Phenotype can also be affected by the environment, but in these single gene examples we assume it is controlled only by the alleles.

callouts.p: The alleles that an organism has for a particular characteristic.
The observable characteristics of an organism, which result from its genotype and the environment.

core.p: Examiners award marks for each stage of a genetic diagram, so always use the same clear layout. Work from the parents down to the offspring and label every row.
bullets: 1. **Parent phenotypes** (e.g. black x white).
2. **Parent genotypes** (e.g. BB x bb).
3. **Gametes**: write each possible allele, ideally in a circle, one allele per gamete.
4. **Offspring genotypes**: combine every gamete from one parent with every gamete from the other.
5. **Offspring phenotypes** matched to each genotype.
6. **Ratio, probability or percentage** if asked.
Gametes must show **single** alleles; writing Bb as a gamete loses the mark.

callouts.p: Write the words parents, gametes, offspring genotypes and offspring phenotypes beside each row. A correct answer with no labels can still lose marks because the examiner cannot see your reasoning.
