core.p: A **Punnett square** is a grid that shows every possible way the gametes from two parents can combine. The gametes of one parent go along the top and the gametes of the other parent go down the side; each box is one possible offspring genotype. Each box has an **equal probability** (one in four for a 2 x 2 square).
bullets: Draw the gametes outside the grid, not inside it.
Fill each box with one allele from its column and one from its row.
Write the dominant allele first in each box (Bb, not bB) to make counting easier.
Count boxes to get the **genotype ratio**, then convert to the **phenotype ratio**.
A Punnett square shows probability for **each** offspring; it does not mean a family of four children will be exactly 3 : 1.

callouts.p: Bb x Bb always gives genotypes 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, and phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

core.h: The three key crosses to know
core.p: Almost every exam question is a version of one of these crosses. Knowing the outcomes lets you check your diagram quickly.
bullets: **BB x bb**: all offspring Bb, all dominant phenotype.
**Bb x Bb**: 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb; 3 dominant : 1 recessive (75% : 25%).
**Bb x bb**: 1 Bb : 1 bb; 1 dominant : 1 recessive (50% : 50%).
BB x Bb: 1 BB : 1 Bb; all dominant phenotype.
bb x bb: all bb; all recessive phenotype.

callouts.p: If offspring show a 3 : 1 ratio, both parents were heterozygous. If they show 1 : 1, one parent was heterozygous and the other homozygous recessive.

core.h: Test cross: finding an unknown genotype
core.p: An organism with the dominant phenotype could be BB or Bb. To find out, breed it with a **homozygous recessive** (bb) organism. The recessive parent can only give b, so the offspring phenotypes reveal which alleles the unknown parent passed on.
bullets: If **all** offspring show the dominant phenotype, the unknown parent is most likely **BB**.
If **any** offspring show the recessive phenotype, the unknown parent **must be Bb**, because a bb offspring needs a b allele from each parent.
Expect about 1 : 1 if the parent is Bb.
Larger numbers of offspring give a more reliable conclusion; a small litter could all be dominant by chance even if the parent is Bb.

callouts.p: A single offspring with the recessive phenotype proves that both parents carry at least one recessive allele.

core.p: A **family pedigree** (family tree) shows how a characteristic or genetic disorder is inherited through several generations. Each person is a symbol, so you can follow alleles from parents to children.
bullets: **Square** = male; **circle** = female.
**Shaded** symbol = has the characteristic or disorder (affected); **unshaded** = unaffected.
Some pedigrees use a half shaded symbol or a dot for a **carrier**.
A **horizontal line** between a male and a female = they are parents together.
A **vertical line** down from that leads to their children, who hang from a horizontal sibling line.
Generations are often numbered with Roman numerals (I, II, III) and individuals with numbers.
Always read the **key** given in the question.

core.p: Pedigree questions ask you to work out genotypes and explain how you know. Start with the people whose genotype is certain, then work outwards.
bullets: Anyone showing a **recessive** characteristic must be **homozygous recessive** (ff).
If two **unaffected** parents have an **affected** child, the condition is **recessive** and both parents must be **heterozygous** (Ff): each passed on one f allele.
An unaffected child of two carriers could be FF or Ff; you cannot tell from the pedigree alone (probability 2 in 3 of being a carrier).
Every child of an affected (ff) parent receives an f allele, so an unaffected child of an ff parent must be Ff.
If two **affected** parents have an **unaffected** child, the condition must be caused by a **dominant** allele and both parents are heterozygous.

callouts.p: For 'explain how you know' marks, link the evidence to the genotype: 'II-4 is affected so must be ff; she received one f allele from each parent, so I-1 and I-2 must both be Ff because they are unaffected.'

core.p: **Cystic fibrosis** is caused by a **recessive** allele. It affects cell membranes, so thick, sticky mucus builds up in the lungs and digestive system. Only people with two recessive alleles (ff) have the disorder; heterozygous people (Ff) are **carriers** with no symptoms.
bullets: Two carriers (Ff x Ff): 1 in 4 (25%) chance each child has cystic fibrosis.
Two carriers: 1 in 2 (50%) chance each child is a carrier.
Carrier x non-carrier (Ff x FF): no children affected, but 50% chance each child is a carrier.
Recessive disorders can appear to **skip generations** because carriers pass the allele on without showing it.

core.p: **Polydactyly** (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a **dominant** allele, D. Only one copy is needed to have the condition, so a person with Dd has polydactyly. There are no symptomless carriers of a dominant allele.
bullets: Dd x dd: 50% chance each child has polydactyly.
Dd x Dd: 75% chance each child has polydactyly.
Dominant conditions usually appear in **every generation**, because anyone with the allele shows it.
Unaffected people with a dominant disorder in the family are dd and cannot pass it on.

core.p: Each fertilisation is an **independent random event**. Which sperm fertilises which egg is down to chance, so the outcome for one child does not affect the next. Genetic diagrams give the **probability** for each offspring; actual families, especially small ones, often do not match the predicted ratio.
bullets: A 1 in 4 chance means 1 in 4 for **every** child, even if the first child was already affected.
The larger the number of offspring (e.g. hundreds of pea plants), the closer the results get to the expected ratio.
Ratios can be written as a ratio (3 : 1), fraction (3/4), percentage (75%) or decimal (0.75).

callouts.p: Two carriers who have three unaffected children do NOT have a guaranteed affected fourth child. The chance is still 1 in 4.

analogy.p: Each parent is like a person holding two cards for one gene, for example a black card (B) and a white card (b). To make a child, each parent shuffles and hands over just one card at random, so the child ends up with a new two-card hand. A black card always 'wins' the display when it is present, so you only see white if both cards are white. A Punnett square is simply a list of every possible pair of cards that could be handed over. Where it breaks down: real alleles are DNA sequences, not cards, and dominance happens because the dominant allele usually codes for a working protein while the recessive one does not; also, in real organisms phenotype can be affected by many genes and the environment.

terms.d: A section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein.
A different version of the same gene.
A long coiled molecule of DNA carrying many genes, found in the nucleus.
A sex cell (sperm or egg) containing one allele of each gene (haploid).
An allele that is expressed in the phenotype when only one copy is present.
An allele that is only expressed in the phenotype when two copies are present (no dominant allele).
Having two identical alleles of a gene, e.g. BB or bb.
Having two different alleles of a gene, e.g. Bb.
The combination of alleles an organism has for a characteristic.
The observable characteristic produced by the genotype (and environment).
A cross that follows the inheritance of one characteristic controlled by a single gene.
A grid used to show all possible combinations of gametes from two parents and the probability of each offspring genotype.
A labelled diagram showing parent phenotypes and genotypes, gametes, and offspring genotypes and phenotypes.
A diagram showing how a characteristic is inherited by members of a family over several generations.
A heterozygous person who has one recessive allele for a disorder but does not have the disorder.
Crossing an organism with the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive organism to find its genotype.

mistakes.w: Gametes written as Bb or BB.
mistakes.r: Each gamete contains only ONE allele of each gene, e.g. B or b.

mistakes.w: A dominant allele is the one most people have.
mistakes.r: A dominant allele is expressed when only one copy is present; it says nothing about how common it is.

mistakes.w: Using C and c, or S and s, so the examiner cannot tell them apart.
mistakes.r: Use letters whose capital and lower case look different, or follow the letters given in the question.

mistakes.w: Bb x Bb gives a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio of black to white.
mistakes.r: 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotype ratio (BB : Bb : bb); the phenotype ratio is 3 black : 1 white.

mistakes.w: If the first child of two carriers has cystic fibrosis, the next three will not.
mistakes.r: Each fertilisation is independent; every child has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance.

mistakes.w: An unaffected person in a family with a recessive disorder must be homozygous dominant.
mistakes.r: They could be homozygous dominant or heterozygous (a carrier); you need more evidence to decide.

mistakes.w: Heterozygous means having two recessive alleles.
mistakes.r: Heterozygous means having two different alleles; two recessive alleles is homozygous recessive.

mistakes.w: Stating parent genotypes from a pedigree without any reason.
mistakes.r: Explain using evidence: an affected child of unaffected parents shows both parents passed on a recessive allele, so both are heterozygous.

mistakes.w: Putting the gametes inside the Punnett square boxes.
mistakes.r: Gametes go along the top and side; the boxes contain the offspring genotypes.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term heterozygous.
model: Having two different alleles of a gene (e.g. Bb).
exam.tip: Do not say 'different genes'; it is different alleles of the same gene.

exam.q: Explain why an animal with the genotype Bb has black fur when B is the allele for black fur and b is the allele for white fur.
model: B is dominant / b is recessive.
Only one copy of a dominant allele is needed for it to be expressed / the recessive allele is masked.
exam.tip: Two ideas: name which allele is dominant, then explain what dominant means.

exam.q: Two heterozygous pea plants with purple flowers (Pp) are crossed. White flowers are recessive. Use a Punnett square to show the possible genotypes of the offspring and state the ratio of purple to white flowers.
model: Gametes shown as P and p from each parent.
Correct offspring genotypes PP, Pp, Pp, pp.
Phenotypes identified: PP and Pp purple, pp white.
Ratio 3 purple : 1 white.
exam.tip: Label gametes and offspring, and give the phenotype ratio, not the genotype ratio.

exam.q: A homozygous black mouse (BB) is crossed with a white mouse (bb). Give the genotype and phenotype of all the offspring.
model: All offspring Bb.
All offspring black.
exam.tip: Each parent can only make one type of gamete, so there is only one possible offspring genotype.

exam.q: Describe how a breeder could find out whether a black dog is homozygous (BB) or heterozygous (Bb).
model: Breed the black dog with a white / homozygous recessive (bb) dog.
Observe the phenotypes of the puppies.
If any puppies are white, the black dog must be Bb.
If all of a large number of puppies are black, the dog is probably BB.
exam.tip: Mention a large number of offspring to make the conclusion reliable.

exam.q: In a pedigree, two parents without cystic fibrosis have a daughter with cystic fibrosis. Explain what this shows about the inheritance of cystic fibrosis and the genotypes of the parents.
model: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele.
The daughter must be homozygous recessive (ff) / has two recessive alleles.
She received one recessive allele from each parent, so both parents are heterozygous (Ff) / carriers.
exam.tip: Link each statement to the evidence in the pedigree.

exam.q: State what a square and a shaded circle represent in a family pedigree.
model: Square = male.
Shaded circle = female who has the characteristic / is affected.
exam.tip: Always check the key: some papers shade carriers differently.

exam.q: A man who is heterozygous for polydactyly (Dd) has children with a woman who does not have polydactyly (dd). Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele. Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their children.
model: Parent genotypes Dd and dd.
Gametes D and d from father; d and d from mother.
Offspring genotypes Dd, Dd, dd, dd.
Phenotypes: Dd polydactyly, dd unaffected (1 : 1).
exam.tip: Set out every row: parents, gametes, offspring genotypes, offspring phenotypes.

exam.q: Explain why recessive genetic disorders can appear to skip a generation in a family pedigree.
model: Heterozygous people / carriers have the recessive allele but do not show the disorder.
Carriers can pass the allele to their children, who can be affected if they receive a recessive allele from both parents.
exam.tip: Use the word carrier and say that both parents must pass on the allele.

exam.q: Explain, using genetic diagrams, how two parents with brown eyes can have a child with blue eyes, but two parents with blue eyes cannot have a child with brown eyes. Assume eye colour is controlled by one gene in which brown (B) is dominant to blue (b).
model: Blue eyes is the recessive phenotype, so a blue-eyed person must be bb.
Brown-eyed parents can be heterozygous (Bb).
Bb x Bb gametes B, b and B, b give BB, Bb, Bb, bb.
So there is a 1 in 4 / 25% chance of a bb child with blue eyes.
Blue-eyed parents are both bb and can only make b gametes.
All children are bb, so none can have brown eyes (no B allele to inherit).
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer needs both crosses shown and a clear conclusion for each.

worked.q: In guinea pigs, rough coat (R) is dominant to smooth coat (r). Two rough-coated guinea pigs have 12 offspring: 9 rough and 3 smooth. Deduce the parents' genotypes and show the cross.
steps: Smooth offspring are rr, so each received an r allele from each parent.
Both parents are rough, so each has at least one R; therefore both are Rr.
Parents: Rr x Rr. Gametes: R, r and R, r.
Punnett square: RR, Rr, Rr, rr.
Expected phenotype ratio 3 rough : 1 smooth; 12 offspring x 3/4 = 9 rough and 12 x 1/4 = 3 smooth, matching the results.
worked.ans: Both parents are heterozygous (Rr); the 9 : 3 result is exactly the 3 : 1 ratio expected.

worked.q: Use the cystic fibrosis pedigree (I-1 and I-2 unaffected; daughter II-4 affected; sons II-3 and II-5 unaffected) to give the genotypes of I-1, I-2, II-4 and the possible genotypes of II-3. Use F and f.
steps: II-4 is affected; cystic fibrosis is recessive, so II-4 is ff.
II-4 inherited one f from each parent.
I-1 and I-2 are unaffected, so each must also have an F: both are Ff.
Ff x Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. II-3 is unaffected, so he is FF or Ff.
Among unaffected children, 2 of the 3 possible combinations are Ff.
worked.ans: I-1 = Ff, I-2 = Ff, II-4 = ff, II-3 = FF or Ff (2/3 chance he is a carrier).

worked.q: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype (T = tall, t = dwarf) is crossed with a dwarf plant. The cross produces 48 tall and 52 dwarf plants. What is the genotype of the tall parent?
steps: The dwarf parent must be tt and can only make t gametes.
Dwarf offspring (tt) appeared, so the tall parent must have given a t allele.
Tall parent is therefore Tt.
Tt x tt gives Tt, Tt, tt, tt: expected ratio 1 tall : 1 dwarf.
48 : 52 is very close to 1 : 1; the small difference is due to chance in fertilisation.
worked.ans: The tall parent is heterozygous, Tt.

bio_edx.2.9.summary: In humans, sex is determined by one pair of chromosomes, the **sex chromosomes**: females are **XX** and males are **XY**. Every egg carries an X chromosome, but half of sperm carry an X and half carry a Y, so it is the **sperm that determines the sex** of the baby at fertilisation. A genetic diagram or Punnett square of XX x XY shows that there is always a **50% (1 in 2) chance** of a boy or a girl for each pregnancy.

core.p: Human body cells contain **46 chromosomes** arranged in **23 pairs**. Twenty-two of these pairs are the same in males and females and are called **autosomes**. The 23rd pair are the **sex chromosomes**, which determine whether a person is male or female.
bullets: Females have two **X chromosomes**: **XX**.
Males have one **X** and one **Y chromosome**: **XY**.
The **Y chromosome** is much smaller than the X and carries far fewer genes.
The Y chromosome carries a gene that causes the embryo to develop **testes**; without it, ovaries develop.
Body cells are **diploid** (two sets of chromosomes, 46); gametes are **haploid** (one set, 23).

callouts.p: The pair of chromosomes (X and Y) that determine the sex of an individual: XX in females and XY in males.

core.p: Gametes are made by **meiosis**, which halves the chromosome number so each gamete gets **one** chromosome from each pair, including **one sex chromosome**.
bullets: A woman (XX) can only pass on an X, so **every egg contains an X chromosome**.
A man (XY) passes on either his X or his Y, so **50% of sperm carry X and 50% carry Y**.
Which sex chromosome goes into a sperm is random, so roughly equal numbers of X and Y sperm are made.
This is why the father, not the mother, determines the sex of the child.

callouts.p: The sex of a baby is determined by whether the egg is fertilised by an X-carrying or a Y-carrying sperm.

fig.cap: The X chromosome is much larger than the Y. A woman's body cells contain two X chromosomes; a man's contain one X and one Y. Each gamete receives just one sex chromosome.

core.p: At **fertilisation** the nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an egg, forming a **zygote** with 46 chromosomes again. The sex chromosome in the sperm decides the sex chromosomes of the zygote.
bullets: Egg (X) + X sperm = **XX zygote**: develops into a **girl**.
Egg (X) + Y sperm = **XY zygote**: develops into a **boy**.
The sex is therefore fixed at the moment of fertilisation.
Fertilisation is random: any sperm could reach the egg first.

callouts.p: The fusion of the nucleus of a male gamete with the nucleus of a female gamete to form a zygote.

core.p: Sex determination is set out in exactly the same way as any monohybrid cross, but the **chromosomes X and Y** are written instead of alleles.
bullets: Parent phenotypes: female x male.
Parent genotypes (sex chromosomes): XX x XY.
Gametes: X and X from the mother; X and Y from the father.
Offspring: XX, XX, XY, XY.
Offspring phenotypes: 2 female : 2 male.
Ratio 1 : 1; probability of a girl = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.

callouts.p: Write X and Y in separate gamete circles. Writing 'XY' as a sperm loses the gamete mark.

core.p: A Punnett square gives the same result in a compact form. Put the father's sperm (X and Y) along the top and the mother's eggs (X and X) down the side.
bullets: Two of the four boxes are XX and two are XY.
Each box has a 1 in 4 chance, so XX = 2/4 = 1/2.
The mother's gametes are identical, so you could even draw a 1 x 2 grid: X egg with X sperm or Y sperm.
Always state the ratio and say which genotype is male and which is female.

callouts.p: For every pregnancy the probability of a boy is 0.5 (50%) and the probability of a girl is 0.5 (50%).

fig.cap: Punnett square for XX x XY. Two boxes are XX (female) and two are XY (male), giving a 1 : 1 ratio and a 50% chance of either sex for every child.

core.p: Each fertilisation is an **independent random event**. The X and Y sperm are produced in equal numbers and either is equally likely to fertilise the egg, so previous children do not change the chance for the next one.
bullets: A couple with three girls still has a **50%** chance of a boy next time.
Across a whole population, the numbers of boys and girls born are roughly equal.
In a small family, actual results often differ from 1 : 1 just by chance.
Probability of a specific sequence multiplies: two girls in a row = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

callouts.p: Never say a couple with several boys is 'more likely' or 'due' to have a girl. Each pregnancy is 50 : 50.

core.p: Sex determination is not controlled by a dominant and recessive allele pair. It depends on **whole chromosomes**: having a Y chromosome (with its testis-determining gene) makes a person male.
bullets: In a normal monohybrid cross you write alleles (B, b).
In sex determination you write chromosomes (X, Y).
X and Y are not 'dominant' or 'recessive'; do not use these words for them.
The layout of the diagram (parents, gametes, offspring, ratio) is exactly the same.

core.p: During **meiosis** in the testes, the X and Y chromosomes are separated into different cells. This is why a man produces two types of sperm in equal numbers. In the ovaries both X chromosomes are identical in type, so only X eggs are made.
bullets: Meiosis produces **four haploid gametes** from one cell.
In males, two of the four sperm get the X and two get the Y.
Each gamete contains 22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome.
Fertilisation restores the diploid number (46) and a pair of sex chromosomes.

callouts.p: A cell with one set of chromosomes (23 in humans), such as a gamete.

core.h: Using sex determination in probability questions
core.p: Exam questions sometimes combine sex determination with another characteristic, asking for the probability of, for example, 'a girl with cystic fibrosis'. Work out each probability separately and **multiply** them, because the two events are independent.
bullets: Probability of a girl = 1/2.
Probability of cystic fibrosis from two carriers = 1/4.
Probability of a girl with cystic fibrosis = 1/2 x 1/4 = 1/8 (12.5%).
Only multiply when the question asks for both things together.

callouts.p: 'What is the probability that their next child is a boy?' is just 1/2. 'What is the probability that their next child is a boy with the condition?' needs multiplying.

core.p: Higher-mark questions ask you to explain why the father determines the sex, or why the ratio is 1 : 1. A grade 9 answer links chromosomes, meiosis, gametes, fertilisation and probability in a logical chain.
bullets: State the sex chromosomes: female XX, male XY.
Explain that meiosis gives one sex chromosome per gamete.
All eggs carry X; half of sperm carry X and half Y.
Fertilisation by an X sperm gives XX (female); by a Y sperm gives XY (male).
Fertilisation is random so the probability of each is 50%.
Support with a correctly labelled genetic diagram or Punnett square.

analogy.p: Imagine the mother has a bag containing only X tickets and the father has a bag with equal numbers of X and Y tickets. A baby is made by drawing one ticket from each bag. Because the mother's ticket is always X, the father's ticket alone decides the result: X gives XX (girl), Y gives XY (boy), each with a 50% chance. Where it breaks down: tickets are put back in a bag, while each gamete is a real cell made by meiosis; and it is the Y chromosome's gene triggering testis development, not simply having a letter, that makes the embryo male.

terms.d: A long, coiled molecule of DNA carrying many genes, found in the nucleus.
The pair of chromosomes that determine sex: XX in females, XY in males.
The 22 pairs of chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes.
The larger sex chromosome; females have two, males have one.
The smaller sex chromosome found only in males; carries a gene that causes testes to develop.
A haploid sex cell (sperm or egg) containing one chromosome from each pair.
Having one set of chromosomes (23 in humans).
Having two sets of chromosomes (46 in humans, in 23 pairs).
Cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes.
The fusion of a male and a female gamete nucleus to form a zygote.
The diploid cell formed at fertilisation.
A labelled diagram showing parents, gametes and offspring of a cross.
A grid showing every possible combination of gametes from two parents.
The chance of an outcome, expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage.

mistakes.w: The mother decides the sex of the baby.
mistakes.r: The father's sperm decides: all eggs carry X, but sperm carry either X or Y.

mistakes.w: Males are XX and females are XY.
mistakes.r: Females are XX; males are XY.

mistakes.w: Writing the sperm gamete as XY.
mistakes.r: Each gamete contains one sex chromosome: X or Y.

mistakes.w: Some eggs carry a Y chromosome.
mistakes.r: All eggs carry an X chromosome because females have no Y.

mistakes.w: A couple with three boys is more likely to have a girl next.
mistakes.r: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability is still 50%.

mistakes.w: The Y chromosome is dominant.
mistakes.r: X and Y are chromosomes, not alleles; the Y carries a gene that triggers male development.

mistakes.w: Humans have 23 chromosomes in body cells.
mistakes.r: Body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); gametes have 23.

mistakes.w: The ratio of boys to girls is 2 : 2 so the probability is 2.
mistakes.r: The ratio simplifies to 1 : 1 and the probability is 1/2, 0.5 or 50%.

exam.q: State the sex chromosomes found in the body cells of a human female.
model: XX.
exam.tip: One mark: give both letters.

exam.q: State the number of chromosomes in a human sperm cell.
exam.tip: Gametes are haploid, half of 46.

exam.q: Give the two possible sex chromosomes found in human sperm cells.
model: X.
Y.
exam.tip: Sperm carry one or the other, never both.

exam.q: Explain why all human eggs contain an X chromosome.
model: Females have two X chromosomes / are XX.
Meiosis gives each egg one sex chromosome, which must be X.
exam.tip: Link the female genotype to the gametes.

exam.q: Draw a Punnett square to show how sex is inherited in humans and state the probability that a child will be male.
model: Mother's gametes X and X; father's gametes X and Y.
Offspring XX, XX, XY, XY.
XX identified as female and XY as male.
Probability of male = 1/2 / 0.5 / 50%.
exam.tip: Label which parent the gametes come from and which genotype is which sex.

exam.q: A couple already have two daughters. State the probability that their next child will be a son, and explain your answer.
model: Each fertilisation is independent / random, so earlier children do not affect the next one.
exam.tip: The trap is to suggest a higher chance of a boy.

exam.q: Explain how the sex of a baby is determined at fertilisation.
model: The egg always contains an X chromosome.
The sperm contains either an X or a Y chromosome.
X sperm gives XX (girl); Y sperm gives XY (boy).
exam.tip: Use the word fertilisation and state both outcomes.

exam.q: Calculate the probability that a couple's first two children will both be girls.
model: Probability of each girl = 1/2.
exam.tip: Independent events: multiply the probabilities.

exam.q: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis. Calculate the probability that their next child will be a boy with cystic fibrosis.
model: Probability of cystic fibrosis = 1/4.
Probability of boy = 1/2.
exam.tip: Work out each part separately, then multiply.

exam.q: Explain why approximately equal numbers of boys and girls are born in a population. Use a genetic diagram in your answer.
model: Females are XX and males are XY.
Meiosis produces gametes with one sex chromosome each.
All eggs carry X.
Half the sperm carry X and half carry Y.
Correct genetic diagram showing XX, XX, XY, XY.
Fertilisation is random so there is a 1 : 1 ratio / 50% chance of each sex.
exam.tip: Include a fully labelled diagram and finish with the probability.

worked.q: Show, using a genetic diagram, the expected ratio of male to female offspring for a human couple.
steps: Parent phenotypes: female x male.
Parent genotypes: XX x XY.
Gametes: mother X, X; father X, Y.
Offspring genotypes: XX, XY, XX, XY.
Phenotypes: XX = female, XY = male.
Ratio 2 female : 2 male, which simplifies to 1 : 1.
worked.ans: 1 male : 1 female; probability of either sex = 0.5 (50%).

worked.q: A family has four children. What is the probability that all four are boys?
steps: Probability of a boy for each child = 1/2, independent of other children.
Probability of four boys = 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2.
As a percentage: 1 / 16 x 100 = 6.25%.

worked.q: A hospital records 1000 births in a year: 508 boys and 492 girls. Explain whether this supports the idea that sex is determined by a 1 : 1 ratio of X and Y sperm.
steps: Expected from the genetic diagram: 50% boys = 500 and 50% girls = 500.
Observed 508 : 492 is very close to 500 : 500.
The small difference is due to fertilisation being random.
A large sample (1000) makes the result reliable.
worked.ans: Yes: the observed ratio (about 1.03 : 1) is close to the expected 1 : 1, with small differences explained by chance.

bio_edx.2.14.summary: The **Human Genome Project (HGP)** was an international project, completed in 2003, that worked out the **sequence of all the bases** in human DNA (about 3 billion base pairs) and located roughly **20,000 to 25,000 genes**. Knowing where genes are and which alleles are linked to disease lets doctors **test for inherited disorders**, predict risk of diseases such as some cancers, and develop **personalised medicine** so that the right drug and dose are matched to a person's genome. These benefits come with **ethical and practical concerns**, such as discrimination, anxiety and the fact that a risk allele does not mean a person will definitely get the disease.

core.h: What the Human Genome Project was
core.p: The **genome** is the entire genetic material of an organism. The HGP set out to read the **order of bases (A, T, C, G)** along all the DNA in a human cell and to find where every gene is.
bullets: Began in **1990**; a draft was announced in **2000** and the sequence was declared complete in **2003**.
An **international collaboration**: scientists in many countries (including the UK, USA, France, Germany, Japan and China) shared the work.
Data were made **freely available** to scientists worldwide, so research groups everywhere could use them.
It sequenced roughly **3 billion base pairs** across the 23 pairs of chromosomes.
The DNA used came from a small number of anonymous volunteers, so the result is a **reference genome**, not one person's exact DNA.

callouts.p: The entire genetic material of an organism.
To sequence all the bases in the human genome and identify the location of all human genes.

core.p: The HGP produced a map of human DNA that scientists still use. Its outcomes are what exam questions mean when they ask what the project achieved.
bullets: The **complete base sequence** of the human genome was published.
Around **20,000 to 25,000 genes** were identified, far fewer than the 100,000 scientists had expected.
The **position of genes on each chromosome** was mapped.
Scientists found that only a small percentage (about **1 to 2%**) of human DNA codes for proteins; much is **non-coding DNA**.
Genes and alleles linked to over **1,800 inherited diseases** have been located, helped by HGP data.
It showed that humans share most of their DNA; small **variations** between people explain differences in characteristics and disease risk.
It speeded up DNA sequencing technology, so sequencing is now **much faster and cheaper**.

callouts.p: If asked for outcomes, give what was found or made possible (sequence known, genes located, disease alleles identified), not just 'it helped medicine'.

core.p: Once scientists know where a gene is and what its normal base sequence is, they can compare a patient's DNA to the reference and spot **alleles that cause or increase the risk of disease**.
bullets: A gene **codes for a specific protein**; a faulty allele can produce a faulty protein or none at all.
Comparing many people's genomes links particular **variants** to particular diseases.
This explains **why** some disorders run in families and allows doctors to predict who is at risk.
Understanding the faulty protein helps researchers **design drugs** that target the cause, not just the symptoms.

core.h: Use 1: Genetic testing for inherited disorders
core.p: A **genetic test** looks for a particular allele in a person's DNA. HGP data tell scientists which allele to look for and where it is.
bullets: Tests can diagnose **inherited disorders** such as **cystic fibrosis** or **Huntington's disease**.
Adults can find out if they are **carriers** of a recessive allele before deciding to have children.
Embryos can be screened (for example during IVF) or a fetus tested during pregnancy.
Early diagnosis means treatment or lifestyle changes can **start sooner**, improving outcomes.
A positive result for a recessive disorder in both parents allows a couple to understand the **probability** of an affected child.

callouts.p: Genetic testing is only possible because the HGP identified which genes and alleles are linked to which disorders.

core.p: Some alleles do not cause a disease directly but **increase the risk** of developing it. Knowing this lets people reduce other risk factors.
bullets: Example: certain alleles of the **BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes** greatly increase the risk of **breast and ovarian cancer**.
People with a high-risk allele can have **more frequent screening** (such as mammograms) or choose preventative surgery.
Risk alleles for **heart disease** or type 2 diabetes can encourage lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise.
Most common diseases are affected by **many genes and the environment**, so a risk allele is a probability, not a certainty.

callouts.p: Having a risk allele does NOT mean a person will definitely get the disease. Say it increases the probability or risk.

core.p: **Personalised medicine** means choosing treatments to suit an individual's genome. People respond differently to the same drug because of small differences in their alleles.
bullets: Some alleles change how quickly the body **breaks down a drug**, so the best **dose** varies between people.
Some drugs only work, or only work well, in people with a particular variant.
Testing first means the patient gets the **most effective drug at the right dose** first time.
This reduces **side effects** and adverse reactions.
It saves time and money because ineffective drugs are not prescribed.
In cancer, the DNA of the **tumour** can be sequenced to choose a drug that targets its particular mutation.

callouts.p: Medical treatment tailored to a person's genetic make-up, so the most effective drug and dose can be chosen.

core.p: Knowing the gene and the protein it codes for helps scientists understand exactly **what goes wrong** in a disease.
bullets: New drugs can be designed to target the **faulty protein** or the process it affects.
It supports research into **gene therapy**, where a working allele is added to cells to correct a disorder.
Comparing tumour DNA with normal DNA helps identify which mutations drive a **cancer**.
It helps researchers understand **inherited disorders** whose causes were previously unknown.

core.p: The genome data have uses outside the clinic, which can appear in 'other uses' questions.
bullets: Tracing **human evolution and migration** by comparing DNA from different populations.
Improved **DNA profiling** methods for forensic science.
Comparing human genes with those of other species shows **evolutionary relationships**.

core.p: Exam answers often need a balanced list of advantages. Each one should say what is possible **and why it helps**.
bullets: Earlier and more accurate **diagnosis** of genetic disorders.
People at risk can take **preventative action** or have regular screening.
Carriers can make **informed decisions** about having children.
**More effective treatment** with fewer side effects through personalised medicine.
Faster development of **new drugs** and possible gene therapies.

core.p: Being able to read a person's genome raises important questions about **who should know** and **what they should do** with the information.
bullets: **Discrimination**: employers or insurance companies might refuse jobs or charge more if they knew a person's genetic risks.
**Anxiety and stress**: knowing you have a high-risk allele, or an incurable disorder like Huntington's, can cause worry, even if you never develop the disease.
**False reassurance**: not having a known risk allele does not mean you are safe, because environment and other genes matter.
**False positives or negatives** in tests can lead to wrong decisions.
**Privacy**: genetic data must be stored securely; it also reveals information about relatives who did not agree to be tested.
Many disorders still have **no cure**, so knowledge may not lead to treatment.
Testing and personalised drugs can be **expensive** and not available to everyone.
Embryo screening raises worries about choosing characteristics ('designer babies').

callouts.p: In evaluate questions, give benefits AND drawbacks, then finish with a justified conclusion.

core.p: A table helps you build balanced 6 mark answers.
bullets: Pair each benefit with a matching concern to show balance.
Use specific examples (cystic fibrosis, BRCA, drug dose) to gain the higher marks.

core.h: Linking the idea to genes and alleles
core.p: To get top marks, connect the HGP to what you know about DNA: the project identified **genes**, and different **alleles** of those genes give different proteins and phenotypes.
bullets: Genome sequence → identify genes → identify alleles linked to disease → test patients for those alleles.
Use the words **gene, allele, base sequence and genome** correctly; mark schemes reward them.
Remember that many characteristics, and many diseases, are controlled by **several genes** plus the environment.

callouts.p: The HGP did not 'cure' diseases. It provides information that makes diagnosis and new treatments possible.

analogy.t: A complete instruction manual with an index
analogy.p: Before the HGP, the human body's instruction manual existed but no one had read every letter or made an index. The HGP read all 3 billion letters and listed where each instruction (gene) starts. Now a doctor with a broken machine (a patient) can look up the right page, spot a misprint (a disease allele) and pick the repair that suits that copy of the manual (personalised medicine). The analogy breaks down because a real manual's misprint always causes the same fault, whereas many alleles only change the risk of disease, and the environment also affects whether the body 'breaks'. Also, everyone's manual is slightly different; the HGP reference is a standard copy built from several people.

terms.d: The entire genetic material of an organism.
International project (1990 to 2003) that sequenced all the bases in human DNA and mapped the location of human genes.
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.
A different form of the same gene.
The order of the bases A, T, C and G along a DNA strand.
Working out the order of bases in a piece of DNA.
Analysing a person's DNA to find whether they have a particular allele.
A disorder caused by a faulty allele passed on from parents, for example cystic fibrosis.
A person who has one copy of a recessive allele for a disorder but does not have the disorder.
Treatment tailored to an individual's genome so the most effective drug and dose are used.
An allele that increases the probability of developing a disease but does not make it certain.
Genes in which certain alleles greatly increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
DNA that does not code for proteins; most of the human genome.
Treating a genetic disorder by inserting a working allele into a patient's cells.
Treating people unfairly, for example by employers or insurers, because of their genetic information.

mistakes.w: The Human Genome Project found the genes for every characteristic.
mistakes.r: It sequenced the bases and located the genes; the function of many genes is still unknown.

mistakes.w: If you have the BRCA allele you will get breast cancer.
mistakes.r: The allele increases the risk or probability of developing cancer; it is not certain.

mistakes.w: The HGP cured genetic diseases.
mistakes.r: It provides information that allows diagnosis, screening and development of new treatments.

mistakes.w: Personalised medicine means a doctor talks to the patient to choose a drug.
mistakes.r: The drug and dose are chosen based on the patient's genome or alleles.

mistakes.w: Genome means one gene.
mistakes.r: Genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.

mistakes.w: Genetic testing has no downsides.
mistakes.r: Possible discrimination by employers or insurers, anxiety, false results and privacy issues.

mistakes.w: Humans have about 100,000 genes.
mistakes.r: The HGP found about 20,000 to 25,000 genes.

mistakes.w: The HGP sequenced one person's DNA.
mistakes.r: It produced a reference sequence from DNA of several anonymous volunteers.

exam.q: What is meant by the term genome?
model: The entire genetic material of an organism.
exam.tip: Use the exact definition: entire genetic material.

exam.q: State one outcome of the Human Genome Project.
model: The whole base sequence of human DNA was determined / genes were located on chromosomes / alleles linked to diseases were identified.
exam.tip: One clear outcome is enough; do not list vague 'it helped science'.

exam.q: Describe two outcomes of the Human Genome Project.
model: The sequence of bases in the human genome was worked out.
The location of (around 20,000 to 25,000) human genes was identified / genes linked to disease identified.
exam.tip: Two separate outcomes, one mark each.

exam.q: Explain how the Human Genome Project could help a person whose family has a history of an inherited disorder.
model: The gene / allele for the disorder can be identified.
So a genetic test can show if the person has (or carries) the allele, allowing early treatment or informed decisions about having children.
exam.tip: Link the identified allele to the test and then to a benefit.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by personalised medicine and why it is better for patients.
model: Treatment chosen to suit the person's genome / alleles.
So the most effective drug or dose is given first time with fewer side effects.
exam.tip: Give a meaning and a reason.

exam.q: A woman finds she has an allele that increases her risk of breast cancer. Suggest two actions she could take.
model: Have more frequent screening (for example mammograms) to detect cancer early.
Consider preventative surgery / lifestyle changes to reduce other risk factors.
exam.tip: Actions must follow from knowing the risk.

exam.q: Give two reasons why some people are concerned about genetic testing.
model: Employers / insurance companies might discriminate against people with risk alleles.
Results may cause anxiety / stress, especially if there is no cure; or false results.
exam.tip: Discrimination and anxiety are the most reliable answers.

exam.q: Explain why a person who tests negative for known risk alleles for heart disease could still develop heart disease.
model: Heart disease is affected by many genes, some of which may not yet be identified.
Environmental / lifestyle factors such as diet, smoking and exercise also affect risk.
exam.tip: Mention multiple genes and environment.

exam.q: Describe how information from the Human Genome Project can be used in medicine.
model: Genes / alleles linked to diseases have been located.
Genetic tests can diagnose inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
People at high risk (for example BRCA alleles) can be screened more often / change lifestyle.
Personalised medicine: drug / dose matched to genome, fewer side effects.
Helps develop new drugs targeting faulty proteins / gene therapy.
exam.tip: Four distinct uses, each with a short reason.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of information from the Human Genome Project in medicine.
model: Benefit: alleles linked to inherited disorders identified, so genetic testing allows early diagnosis.
Benefit: people with risk alleles (for example BRCA) can have extra screening or preventative treatment.
Benefit: personalised medicine gives the most effective drug and dose with fewer side effects.
Benefit: helps develop new drugs and gene therapy.
Drawback: discrimination by employers or insurers; privacy of genetic data.
Drawback: anxiety; risk allele does not mean disease is certain; many disorders have no cure; cost.
Conclusion: justified judgement, for example benefits outweigh risks if data are kept private and counselling is given.
exam.tip: Top band needs both sides and a reasoned conclusion.

worked.q: A doctor wants to prescribe a drug that is broken down quickly in people with allele F and slowly in people with allele S. Explain how the Human Genome Project helps the doctor choose a dose.
steps: The HGP located the gene for the enzyme that breaks down the drug and identified its alleles.
The doctor tests the patient's DNA to find which allele they have.
Allele F: drug is removed quickly, so a higher dose may be needed for it to work.
Allele S: drug stays longer, so a lower dose avoids a build-up and side effects.
worked.ans: Testing for the allele lets the dose be personalised so the drug is effective with fewer side effects.

worked.q: Model answer: give one advantage and one disadvantage of offering everyone a test for the BRCA1 allele.
steps: Advantage: people with the allele know they are at higher risk of breast or ovarian cancer.
So they can have regular screening, so any cancer is found early when treatment is more successful.
Disadvantage: a positive result may cause anxiety even though cancer is not certain.
Or insurers might charge more or refuse cover if they had access to the result.
worked.ans: Early detection through screening versus anxiety and possible discrimination.

worked.q: A student says: 'Since the HGP, we can predict exactly which diseases each person will get.' Correct this statement.
steps: The HGP identified genes and alleles linked to disease.
Some disorders, such as cystic fibrosis, are caused by a single gene so can be diagnosed.
Most diseases depend on many genes and environmental factors.
So a test only gives a probability or risk for most diseases.
worked.ans: We can diagnose some single-gene disorders and estimate risk for others, but cannot predict exactly which diseases a person will get.

bio_edx.2.15.summary: Within any population of a species there is usually **extensive genetic variation**, and this variation arises through **mutations**: random changes in the base sequence of DNA that create **new alleles**. **Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype**, some have a **small effect**, and only **rarely** does a single mutation **significantly affect the phenotype**. Mutations in gametes can be passed to offspring, so over time they build up the variety of alleles that makes individuals different and on which natural selection acts.

core.p: Individuals of the same species are not identical. Much of this difference is **genetic variation**: individuals carry different **alleles** of the same genes.
bullets: Every gene can exist in several versions called **alleles**.
A population therefore contains a large mix of alleles, giving **extensive genetic variation**.
Examples: eye colour, blood group, height (also affected by environment).
Sexual reproduction **shuffles** existing alleles into new combinations, but it does not make new alleles.
The **original source** of all new alleles is **mutation**.

callouts.p: There is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species, and this arises through mutations.

core.p: A **mutation** is a **rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA**. Because the base sequence of a gene codes for a protein, changing it can create a **new allele**.
bullets: Mutations happen **spontaneously**, often when DNA is being **copied** before cell division.
They are **random**: they are not caused by the organism 'needing' a change.
They can occur in any cell, but only those in cells that make **gametes** can be **inherited**.
Mutations in body cells affect only that individual (for example some cancers).

callouts.p: A rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA (a gene or chromosome), which can produce a new allele.

core.p: A gene mutation changes one or more bases. The three main types are named by what happens to the base.
bullets: **Substitution**: one base is swapped for another.
**Insertion**: an extra base is added.
**Deletion**: a base is lost.
Insertions and deletions **shift the reading** of every triplet after the change, so they usually alter the protein more than a single substitution.

core.h: What increases the rate of mutation
core.p: Mutations happen naturally at a low rate, but some factors called **mutagens** make them happen **more often**.
bullets: **Ionising radiation**: X-rays, gamma rays and ultraviolet light.
**Chemical mutagens**: for example some chemicals in **tobacco smoke**.
Mutagens damage DNA, increasing the chance of a change in base sequence.
This is why exposure to radiation is limited and smoking increases the risk of cancer.

callouts.p: Mutagens increase the RATE or chance of mutations; mutations still happen without them.

core.p: A mutation in a gamete-producing cell creates a new allele that can be passed to offspring. Over many generations this adds new alleles to the population.
bullets: Mutation → **new allele** → passed on in gametes → spreads through the population if it is not harmful.
Combining these alleles through **meiosis and fertilisation** gives each individual a unique set.
Without mutation there would be no new alleles, so variation would eventually be lost.
Variation produced by mutation is the raw material for **natural selection**.

fig.cap: Random mutations produce new alleles, which are passed on in gametes and build up extensive genetic variation in a population. Mutagens increase how often this happens.

core.h: Most mutations have no effect on phenotype
core.p: The spec says **most genetic mutations have no effect on the phenotype**. The reasons explain why.
bullets: Most of the genome is **non-coding DNA**, so many mutations do not change any protein.
The genetic code has several triplets for the same amino acid, so a substitution may still code for the **same amino acid** (protein unchanged).
A change to an amino acid that is not in an important part of the protein may not change its **shape or function**.
If the mutation creates a **recessive allele**, a heterozygous individual still has a working dominant allele, so the phenotype is unchanged.

callouts.p: Most genetic mutations have no effect on the phenotype; some have a small effect; rarely a single mutation significantly affects the phenotype.

fig.cap: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype, some have a small effect and only rarely does a single mutation have a significant effect.

core.h: Some mutations have a small effect
core.p: Some mutations **slightly change** a protein, giving a small change in phenotype.
bullets: A substitution may change one amino acid, changing protein shape a little.
An enzyme might then work a little faster or slower, or a pigment be slightly different.
Many characteristics (such as height) are controlled by **many genes**, so a change in one gene has only a **small effect**.
Small effects add to the **continuous variation** seen in populations.

core.h: Rarely, one mutation significantly affects phenotype
core.p: Occasionally a single mutation changes a protein so much that the phenotype changes **significantly**.
bullets: If the mutation changes the **active site of an enzyme**, the substrate may no longer fit, so the enzyme stops working.
A structural protein may change shape and stop doing its job.
Example: **sickle cell anaemia** is caused by a single base substitution in the haemoglobin gene, making red blood cells sickle shaped.
Example: **cystic fibrosis** is caused by a mutation in one gene for a membrane protein, producing thick, sticky mucus.
Very rarely a mutation is **beneficial**, for example antibiotic resistance in bacteria, giving a survival advantage.

callouts.p: For a large effect, follow the chain: base sequence changed → amino acid sequence changed → protein shape changed → protein cannot function → phenotype changed.

core.h: Linking mutation to protein and phenotype
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain the **chain of cause and effect** from DNA to characteristic.
bullets: Base sequence of DNA changes.
The **sequence of amino acids** in the protein may change.
The protein **folds into a different shape**.
The protein (for example an enzyme) may **not function** or function differently.
The **phenotype** changes.

bullets: Always say 'most', 'some' and 'rarely' in the right places.
Effects can be harmful, neutral or, rarely, beneficial.

core.p: The effect of a mutation on survival depends on the **environment** as well as the change itself.
bullets: **Neutral**: no effect on survival (most mutations).
**Harmful**: reduces the chance of survival, for example a disorder.
**Beneficial**: increases chance of survival and reproduction in that environment, so the allele becomes more common over generations.
Example: in bacteria, a mutation giving **antibiotic resistance** is beneficial when antibiotics are present.

callouts.p: Mutations are not usually harmful. Most are neutral, with no effect on the phenotype.

analogy.t: Typos in a giant recipe book
analogy.p: Think of the genome as a huge recipe book copied by hand. A mutation is a random typo made while copying. Most typos land in the notes and blank pages (non-coding DNA) or change a word to one with the same meaning, so the dish tastes the same: no effect. Some typos change '2 tsp' to '3 tsp' and the dish tastes slightly different: a small effect. Very rarely a typo turns 'sugar' into 'salt' in a key step and ruins the cake: a large effect. Copies of the book handed to children carry the typos on, so over time different families' books differ: genetic variation. The analogy breaks down because a cook could spot and correct a typo by reading it, whereas organisms do not choose or notice mutations, and the 'success' of a change depends on the environment, not on taste.

terms.d: A rare, random change in the base sequence of DNA.
Differences in the alleles carried by individuals of the same species.
A different form of the same gene, often produced by mutation.
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein.
The observable characteristics of an organism.
The combination of alleles an organism has.
The order of the bases A, T, C and G along DNA, which determines the amino acid order in a protein.
A mutation in which one base is replaced by a different base.
A mutation in which an extra base is added into the DNA sequence.
A mutation in which a base is removed from the DNA sequence.
A factor, such as ionising radiation or certain chemicals, that increases the rate of mutation.
DNA that does not code for a protein.
A mutation that has no effect on the phenotype or survival.
A mutation that increases an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment.
A disorder caused by a single base substitution in the haemoglobin gene, giving sickle-shaped red blood cells.

mistakes.w: Most mutations are harmful.
mistakes.r: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.

mistakes.w: Mutations happen because the organism needs to adapt.
mistakes.r: Mutations are random changes in DNA; they are not caused by need.

mistakes.w: Sexual reproduction creates new alleles.
mistakes.r: Mutation creates new alleles; sexual reproduction makes new combinations of existing alleles.

mistakes.w: A mutation is a change in a chromosome's shape.
mistakes.r: A mutation is a change in the base sequence of DNA.

mistakes.w: All mutations are passed on to children.
mistakes.r: Only mutations in cells that produce gametes can be inherited.

mistakes.w: A mutation always changes the protein.
mistakes.r: A mutation may be in non-coding DNA or code for the same amino acid, so the protein can be unchanged.

mistakes.w: Radiation causes all mutations.
mistakes.r: Mutations occur spontaneously; mutagens such as radiation increase the rate.

mistakes.w: The mutation changes the shape of the amino acid.
mistakes.r: The mutation changes the sequence of amino acids, which changes the shape of the protein.

exam.q: What is a mutation?
model: A (random) change in the base sequence of DNA.
exam.tip: Say 'base sequence of DNA'.

exam.q: State how genetic variation arises in a population.
model: Through mutations (producing new alleles).
exam.tip: The spec answer is mutations.

exam.q: State the effect that most mutations have on the phenotype.
model: No effect.
exam.tip: Most = no effect; some = small; rarely = significant.

exam.q: Give one factor that increases the rate of mutation.
model: Ionising radiation / X-rays / gamma rays / UV light / chemical mutagens such as in tobacco smoke.
exam.tip: Name a specific mutagen.

exam.q: Explain why a mutation in a skin cell cannot be passed to a person's children.
model: Skin cells are body cells, not cells that make gametes.
Only mutations in gametes (sex cells) are passed on at fertilisation.
exam.tip: Link inheritance to gametes.

exam.q: Explain why many mutations have no effect on the phenotype.
model: The mutation may be in non-coding DNA / the new triplet may code for the same amino acid.
So the protein is unchanged / the new allele may be recessive and masked by a dominant allele.
exam.tip: Give a reason and the consequence for the protein.

exam.q: Explain how a single base mutation could stop an enzyme working.
model: Base sequence of the gene changes.
Changes the sequence of amino acids in the protein.
Changes the shape of the enzyme / active site.
Substrate no longer fits the active site, so the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction.
exam.tip: Follow DNA → amino acids → shape → function.

exam.q: Describe the range of effects that mutations can have on the phenotype of an organism.
model: Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.
Because they are in non-coding DNA or do not change the protein.
Some mutations have a small effect, for example slight change in protein shape.
Rarely a single mutation significantly affects the phenotype, for example sickle cell anaemia / cystic fibrosis.
exam.tip: Use 'most', 'some', 'rarely' with an example.

exam.q: Explain the importance of mutation in producing variation in a population of a species.
model: Mutations are random changes in DNA base sequence.
They produce new alleles.
Mutations in gametes are passed to offspring.
Over generations this increases the number of different alleles so there is extensive genetic variation / provides variation for natural selection.
exam.tip: Go from mutation to population, not just to one individual.

exam.q: Discuss how mutations can affect the phenotype of organisms and the importance of mutations to a population.
model: Mutation is a random change in the base sequence of DNA.
Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype: non-coding DNA, same amino acid coded, or recessive allele masked.
Some have a small effect: slight change to protein shape or activity.
Rarely a single mutation has a significant effect: protein cannot function, e.g. sickle cell anaemia.
Mutations produce new alleles; those in gametes are inherited.
So they are the source of extensive genetic variation in a population.
Beneficial mutations (e.g. antibiotic resistance) can become more common by natural selection.
exam.tip: Cover both effects on phenotype and the population-level role.

worked.q: A DNA sequence TAC GGA TCA mutates to TAC GTA TCA. Name the type of mutation and explain how it might affect the protein.
steps: Compare base by base: the fifth base G has been replaced by T.
One base swapped for another, so it is a substitution.
Only one triplet (GGA to GTA) is changed, so at most one amino acid changes.
If the new triplet codes for the same amino acid, or the change is outside an important region, the protein is unchanged.
If it changes an amino acid in the active site, the protein shape could change and stop it working.
worked.ans: Substitution; it may have no effect, a small effect, or rarely a large effect depending on whether the amino acid and protein shape change.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why sickle cell anaemia is an example of a single mutation that significantly affects phenotype.
steps: A single base substitution occurs in the gene for haemoglobin.
This changes one amino acid in the haemoglobin protein.
The haemoglobin changes shape, making red blood cells sickle shaped.
Sickle cells carry less oxygen and can block capillaries, causing pain and tiredness.
worked.ans: One base change alters the protein enough to change the phenotype significantly.

worked.q: A population of beetles includes green and brown individuals. Explain the original source of the different colour alleles.
steps: Colour depends on pigment proteins coded for by genes.
At some point a random mutation changed the base sequence of the colour gene.
This produced a new allele, coding for a different pigment.
The mutation occurred in a gamete-producing cell, so it was inherited and spread through the population.
worked.ans: The different colour alleles originally arose by mutation, which produced new alleles that were then inherited.
